speechtext: Mr. CURRIE moved that the first report of the Joint Committee on the Printing of Parliament be concurred in.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As this report relates to the Printing of Parliament, which involves an expenditure of money, I am afraid I shall have to ask that it be allowed to stand.

The Printing Committee recommend in this report that in future all reports presented in either the Senate or the House of Commons, by the other committees which contain requests fior the printing of reports, .pamphlets, &c., he first submitted to the Committee on Printing. That recommendation should be really unnecessary because, under Rule 64 of the House, a motion for the printing of any paper must be first submitted to the Joint Committee on Printing for report before any action is taken on it. However, an abuse has arisen in the House, and other committees present to the House resolutions accompanying their reports with motions that a certain number of copies of testimony or papers placed before them should be printed and the House has granted such requests. For instance, the Committee on Agriculture recommended that 150,000 copies of Dr. James Robertson's address before them on the matter of conservation should be printed. That would involve an expenditure of something over $15,000. It is a violation of the rutles, there was a slight clash over the matter, and as a result this report is now presented to the House. Whether this motion is necessary 1 do not know, but it is well to pass it, and so remind the chairman and secretaries of committees that this abuse cannot be continued. In 1908 the amount of money required for sessional printing for the House was $85,000, but last session it was

over $250,000. We do mot -wish to be considered parsimonious, but we feel that orders for .any printing of .such magnitude as this should .at leasit be referred to the committee appointed by parliament to pass upon such things.

The inconvenience is' this: A gentleman is appointed as private secretary to a minister, in some cases at least he does not discharge any duties except those incident to his private secretaryship, and the administration of the department is provided for altogether out-106
side of his services. His minister goes out of office and the private secretary remains in the Civil Service. Under the provisions of the Act of 1908, and under the provisions of this amending Act, he is left for the time being without any special duties to perform. And so matters remain until the department can so organize as to make his services available to the country. That is the difficulty [DOT] which was pointed out to me, and it undoubtedly exists. But it exists no more under this amending Act than under the Act of 1908.

I think it is hardly fair to deal with the private secretary by ignoring the fact that he has a special, case. If a member of the civil service has acted -as private secretary to a minister, of course he has received extra consideration. If the minister goes out the private secretary reverts to the salary which he had before he became private secretary. I think that the man who has acted as private secretary to a minister and has been able to fulfil the duties-the somewhat onerous duties-of that position, has thereby acquired an experience and a knowledge that is valuable. Also he has proven himself a man of such capacity as to entitle him to at any raie more consideration than to merely put him back where he was at the beginning of his term of office as private secretary, perhaps four or five years before. While I am aware that that is the position under the law, I understood that the purpose oi this Bill was to recognize in some measure the idea I have taken the liberty of placing before the committee. As I said, I shall be very sorry if the Bill is not put in such a form as to give the private secretary some consideration. I do not ask that when he drops the very onerous duties of private secretary he should receive absolutely the same salary as he had while he was discharging those duties, but I think it is entirely unfair, and not in the reasonable interest of the public service, that the man who has occupied that position and who has acquired an experience which should be of value should, on a change of government, revert to the position he occupied before he was chosen for the position of private secretary. I would ask the Prime Minister to give some further consideration to that side of the case, unless he has already considered it and has absolutely made up-his mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have considered that. Those gentlemen who leave their positions as private secretary, in some cases at least at the present time, are left almost entirely without any duties to perform. We have no disposition whatever to deal otherwise than fairly with them, but we have to take into consideration the circumstance that it is very difficult, if not impossible, in



some of the departments at least, to make any effective utilization of their services. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) says that they revert to the position which they held at first. That, perhaps, is not an absolutely correct way of stating it, because they have received each year a certain increment in their annual salaries under the provisions of the Civil 'Service Act. True, they do lose at the moment, the sum of $600 a year, to which they were entitled, by virtue of being private secretaries. But we cannot very well deal with that without taking into our regard other considerations which I mentioned a moment ago, and which were brought to_ my attention by 'some members of the civil service. I am placing all private secretaries exactly on the same basis, so far as that is concerned. The provisions embodied in this Bill particularly under subsections 2, 3 and 4, had regard to the men who are being appointed now, and I am striking them out. But 1 am prepared at some later date- for I have not had sufficient time to consider the subject thoroughly-to take up the question of dealing not only with these but also with the men who went out- of office as private secretaries, when the government resigned, but who are still members of the oiv-il service. But I do not think it would be possible for me, purely for lack of time, to deal with that matter this session. So far as the secretaries of ministers of the late administration are concerned, the case of only one of them has been brought to my attention, and he is to be provided for in a way that I hope, will be entirely satisfactory.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.

speechtext:
Mr. PELLETIER moved the second reading of Bill (No. 105) to amend the Post Office Act. He said: This Bill is to provide for an improvement in the railway mail -clerk service, which is not at present in -a satisfactory position. The railway mail clerks now receive ia salary of $500 a year on appointment. We have to get them from the outside, and we have a good de-ai of difficulty in getting good men for the reason that they are not paid as they ought to be. This Bill provides for several oases, which I will -briefly explain to the House.
The first clause provides that any person may be employed temporarily as a railway mail clerk for a period of not more than one year at a salary of $500 a year 106§ 5
and mileage allowance. The present law provides for the temporary employment of clerks for a period of only six months. We extend that period to one year. Tfais-gives the clerks two chances instead of one of passing their examination. When we find some of these men to he good employees, understanding their work, we do not want them to go and take other places.. We are allowing them mileage allowance and I am sure that the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux), will agree with me that this is a wise provision. We cannot expect railway mail clerks to do good work at $500 a year at the present cost of: living. Permanent clerks receive a certain mileage, and these men who are in the-service of the department are doing the: same work, but they are not now given any: mileage allowance. It is hoped that the granting of the mileage allowance will help to retain these men in the service. The experience of the department is that if we do not take better care of out employees we are simply training boys who, when they know something about the service, leave the department to take other situations and we thereby lose some of our most promising employees. We intend! to try to keep these men in our employ by paying them decent salaries.
The second clause is one which will appeal to the House. A great number of temporary mail clerks have not passed the examination. The law says that they must pass the examination in order to be appointed permanently. I do not want to reflect on the Civil Service Commissioners, but I will frankly say that I could not pass their examinations nor could many gentlemen in this House. For this very inferior position, and this small salary, men are expected to answer questions which a young man fresh from college might be able to answer, but which a grown up man would be unable to answer. The exPostmaster General and myself have been obliged to take men who have not passed the examination, but who are just as good: as if they had; they know their business, they do it well, but under the present law we are obliged to send them away. I ask the authority of the House to appoint these men permanently if their services have been satisfactory, and if they are recommended by the superintendent and the controller of the Railway Mail Service. They will have to pass only the p^limin-ary examination, and I have no hesitation in saying that the passing of that examination is a sufficient qualification for the position of railway mail clerk. If they pass that examination they will go up-, step by step, to $1,000. They will stop there if they do not pass the full examination. I felt disposed to be even more lenient, but I suppose progress has to be

made little by little, and I think this will appeal to the House as being a just and fair measure, both t-o these railway mail clerks, who have a great deal of heavy work to do, and to the public service.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.
speechtext: I quite agree with the general lines of this Bill and I concur in the remarks just made. The cost of living is increasing immensely. I remember, although I am not very old myself, that some years ago, a man could bring up a family on a salary of $1,000 a year, but now-a-days it is practically impossible to 'do so, living in a modest way. The railway mail clerks are most excellent officers of His Majesty's service, and as I have told the House on many occasions, they have to incur risks in the discharge of their duties, which other civil servants do not incur. They are obliged to travel at all times of the year, during the heat of the summer and the cold of the winter. They have to take ont insurance policies fcr the protection of their families, and they have to contend with difficulties not experienced by other members of the civil service. Will the clause providing for the raising of the salaries of railway mail clerks up to $1,000 if they pass the preliminary examination apply to any railway mail clerk who is in the service at present regardless of the number of years of his service?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.
speechtext: I will treat them well.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.
speechtext:
Having said so much about what is being done in favour of the railway mail clerks, I wish to emphasize once more before this House, the urgent necessity of extending the provisions of the Civil Service Atct to the outside service. It would save my hon. friend or any minister of the Crown much time and worry, if rhere was one general law applied to civil servants, whether they are in the inside or in the outside service.
When I was in the government, I advocated it, speaking for myself only, but there were some who did not believe that this reform should be accomplished then. However, a bold step must be taken some time, and it is time to take it now. The life of a minister is not worth living if, whenever he moves from Ottawa to Montreal or Quebec, he is to be constantly surrounded by a crowd of office seekers, as I understand my hon. friend the Postmaster General is and as I was when I was Postmaster General. Would it not be better to have the same principle of competitive examination for the outside service as we have now for the inside service ? My hon. friend (Mr. Pelletier) was not here before the days of the new Civil Service Act, and I can assure him that he is living in Paradise now, because he will never have so many visi-Mr. PELLETIER.
tors looking for employment as we had before that Act was passed.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.
speechtext: Did my hon. friend receive more visitors than we do now?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.
speechtext: Oh, yes, we were stormed with visitors and letters. That legislation introduced by Mr. Fisher with respect to the inside service afforded a cure for many evils and gave the ministers of the Crown some little time to devote their energies to the business of the country. Under the present Civil Service Law we get a good class of civil servants; the law is known to the people, the minister is bound by it, and his answer to applicants is that he must obey the law. Why not extend this principle of competitive examination to the outside service? What difference is there between an official of the Post Office Department and an official in the post office at Ottawa, or at Montreal, or in the other cities? They both deal with the same matters, they have to perform practically the same duties; in fact I would, say that the postmasters in Montreal and Ottawa must have perhaps more ability than some departmental officials. I can assure my hon. friend that when he proposes to put the outside officials under the Civil Service Act-and judging by the remarks of the Prime Minister to-day the government is contemplating that-it will meet with favour from this side of the House. Let there be one law for the inside and outside service alike, and thus the ministers wiil have more time to work for the country, and they will have to give less time to working for the office seeker.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.- RAILWAY MAIL CLERKS.
speechtext:
I wish to say a word or two with regard to the railway mail service of this Dominion, and, by way of explanation, I may be frank enough to tell the House that I spent four or five years of my life in that service. I am pleased to know that the Postmaster General realizes the importance of that branch of the department under his charge; I am pleased to know that he realizes that he has good and efficient servants in that branch, and I am pleased to know that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has been able to testify from past experience that the railway mail clerks were faithful and efficient officers during the time he was m charge of the department. I would like to refer now to a Bill affecting the railway mail clerks in-

troduced when the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) was Postmaster General, and I do so for the purpose of making a plea for the railway mail clerks and for that reason alone. In my humble judgment the railway mail service has been sadly neglected in the past and the following quotation from the Bill I refer to will, I think show that:
3. Paragraph (a) of section 32 of the said Act is repealed, and in lieu thereof it is enacted that a railway mail clerk shall be appointed on probation for a period of at least one year, at a salary at the rate of five hundred dollars a year, with an additional allowance or mileage, and on the confirmation of his appointment he may be paid at the rate of six hundred dollars a year, and mileage, with annual increases of one hundred dollars up to eight hundred dollars, and an increase of fifty dollars a year thereafter until the maximum of one thousand four hundred dollars is reached.
Now, I want to point out the injustice of that Bill. Whom does it affect? It affected primarily only the men who had been appointed by the late administration, because it will be noticed that the men who had just been a short time in the service received one hundred dollars a year increase instead of fifty dollars a year, and in the second place it affected that class of men who had been in the service practically for a lifetime and who had already reached the maximum salary of twelve hundred. Thus the great backbone of the service the men not included in those two classes received no immediate benefit whatever from that legislation. The men receiving over eight hundred dollars a year and under twelve hundred received, no benefit, because their increase went along at the rate of fifty dollars a year as formerly. I cannot conceive by what process of reasoning any man could decree that a clerk shall receive one hundred dollars a year increase the first year he is in the service when he knows nothing about it whatever, and that after he had been three years in the service and learned the business from start to finish, that that increase should be dropped to fifty dollars a year. That is one phase of the question I cannot understand. I would appeal to the Postmaster General to, if he possibly can see his way clear, right the wrong that was done by this legislation, and a great wrong it is. There is another phase of the question to which I would direct attention. There has been a tendency in past years to place the railway mail service in a lower grade than other post office officials in the outside service. I want to tell the House that the railway mail clerk takes second place to no class of post office employees. There is not a branch of the department in which the men have to work harder or in which more experience is required. Further, it was the first branch of
the post office service in which the employees were forced to go through a very strict examination on the duties of office in order to get their annual increase. Until a few years ago the railway mail service was the only service in which the employees had to undergo a yearly examination and take ninety per cent before they were pronounced entitled to their fifty dollars a year increase. I mention these facts in the hope that the Postmaster General will, when the ease is fairly and squarely presented, take steps to right the injustice that has been done the railway mail clerks who are, I would say, possibly the most faithful officials in his department. It has been claimed that a railway mail clerk received a salary of fourteen hundred dollars a year and mileage, but when you come to consider the question of salary the mileage should not be taken into account because the mileage is paid only by way of compensation for the extra, risk, and the unnatural conditions under which he has to discharge his duties.
I would like to remind the hon. the Postmaster General that only three or four days ago three of his men went down in a wreck in the Toronto division; and I could mention many such cases in that branch of the service. Men go out three or four times a week taking itheir lives in their bands. Surety these men are entitled to more consideration than, mem who work in offices. I hope the case of the railway mail - clerks of this iDoaninion will he looked into thoroughly, and that tliey will receive the justice they deserve; and I am satisfied that they will receive it at the hands of one of the most just and reasonable Postmaster Generals that I think this country ever had.

The limit of $1,000 is for the men wffio have passed the preliminary examination, to distinguish them from those who have passed both examinations, and whose salary does not stop at $1,000.

speechtext: Is the qualifying examination an examination within the department?

speechtext: Especially for the railway mail clerks?

speechtext: Of course.

The reason I ask is that m man who has had experience might not he able to pass the civil service examination, and still be a very well qualified railway mail clerk. Ii it is an examination Into his special qualifications for his work, it is all right; otherwise, I do not think it is.

I may say to my hon. friend that I fully expect before long to go further than this Bill is going. While it is very satisfactory to find that this Bill *is so well received by both sides of the House, it does not go as far as I would have liked it to go. But we have to make (progress little by little. Railway mail clerks are very good men, and I am happy to see that one who started his career as a railway mail clerk, is now a member of the House of Commons, and one of the best. With regard to the qualifying [DOT]examination, if it is kept on the lines on which it exists now, and we extend the *Civil Service Act to the outside service, it will be very difficult for the Postmaster General to find employees. The preliminary examination is all right, but I think the qualifying examination is too severe. It *should be such as a certain number of people will be able to pass. Now we are obliged to go outside of the Civil Service Commission to get employees, because they have none to give us.
You mean for the outside service?
Yes.
You are obliged to violate the law.
Yes, we overstep the law all the time.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1, salaries of clerks,

As I understand the law at present, the railway mail-clerks are required to pass the civil service examination, 'but the department has been in the habit of employing temporarily, persons who have not passed the examinations, upon the understanding that they might suffer dismissal if the examination "were not passed within a year, and now the -minister proposes to take statutory authority for appointing temporarily those who have not passed the examination.
Mr. PELLETIER, It is now done by overstepping the law, and I want the authority of the law to do it.

The explanation of ihe minister clears up a point about which I had some doubt, as a matter of departmental practice. I had assumed that there -was some statutory authority under Mr. PELLETIER.
which mail clerks were employed temporarily. I understand the minister to say that is not so, and this Bill will, for the first time, create such an authority. It is therefore, only confirming a practice which has been in existence in the past.
They are now employed as labourers.

I quite agree as to the desirability of the legislation in that regard. It has always seemed to me to be a hardship that where you have perfectly competent young men who have passed the preliminary Civil Service examination and who perform their duties-onerous and responsible as they are-very efficiently that they should be prevented' from becoming permanent officers (because of having to pass a qualifying examination. That examination, as the Minister says, has undoubtedly been too severe and in my view the Civil Service commissioners or those who prepare these examination papers, with all due deference to them, do not apprehend what ought to be the qualifications of those who offer themselves as candidates. That erudition, or knowledge of technical subjects, such as one acquires at school is not going to make a man who passejs, the preliminary examination for railway mail clerk any more qualified to perform his duties; and the fact that he is not in a position to pass this purely technical qualifying examination ought not to debar him from permanency of employment. In that connection I am aware of a great many cases of hardship which have occurred within the past few years, and I think that the Minister should have some discretionary power. The evil will not be removed if the position of these men, who were admitted to the service temporarily, is confirmed and the hindrances to them getting increases under the Act, which I have mentioned as being a difficulty in the way, is not also removed. I quite agree with the ex-Postmaster General in the proposition that there should be an extension of the civil service reform generally to the outside service. In a great many branches of the outside service, if there were proper examinations, greater efficiency would be secured, and the evils of patronage would be removed to a very great degree. We are all I assume-although there has been a lot of talk about the matter, and we are making but very slight progress towards attaining the desired end-in favour of causing" the civil service to so improve as in some degree to approach the high status the civil service occupies in the mother country. I suppose patronage is an alluring thing to hon. gentlemen opposite, who have been without that privilege for so long, but they will find it becomes a very ere at burden after a while; and I think we ought to reach the stage in this country

when both parties can unite in a reasonable and sensible proposition of civil service reform for the outside service. That is a general proposition which is not rightly before us perhaps at this time, but it is a deduction from what I was anxious to see done with regard to the aptness and the sensible character of the qualifying examination, because some of the papers submitted to men who occupied temporary positions in the railway mail service and who desired to be made permanent, on presenting themselves for examination, have been shown to me, and as a means calculated to test their fitness or capacity for their duties were in my opinion absolutely ridiculous. It would appear impossible that educated people responsible for the civil service of this country would set papers of the kind, and there certainly requires to be a remedy in that respect both as regards the inside and outside service, if civil service reform is going to apply. Men who have been temporarily employed and are reasonably efficient in the discharge of their duties should not be debarred from promotion by failure to pass a technical examination. Provided you get integrity and general capacity on the part of the candidate the examination should take regard of a knowledge of the details of the particular service and the responsibility of the party affected. The possession of the necessary degree of intelligence can be very readily ascertained without exceptional educational test. At the first blush the Bill would seem to propose that one should be a graduate of the Military College, or of some university of Canada, but that is of course only an alternative qualifying position and would really dispense with the necessity of a graduate of either of these institutions having to go up for examination again. I hope that the minister, acting in conjunction with his colleagues, will see that a qualifying examination of a practical character is established, and the present examinations done away with, so that we may have a practical and sensible test of the qualifications of those who seek to enter the service.

As I stated a moment ago, I would not bav-e allowed the provision for a qualifying examination to remain at all, if I did not expect that this question will be dealt with before long, and that provision will be made for an examination calculated to demonstrate the fitness of candidates for positions they seek to fill and the work they are expected to perform. It seems to me that is the whole question in a nutshell.
That is the idea.

Why put questions about irrelevant matters to a man who is. going to sort letters or to become a railway mail clerk? I am strongly of opinion that
the preliminary examination is all that is necessary to test the capacity of a man seeking to become a railway mail clerk. We must not advance too rapidly along the path of progress; this is the first instalment. I shall -come with other instalments if the present law affecting all the departments is not amended. I shall take care of my own railway mail clerks and my own employees in such a way that they will be able to perform their duties efficiently, and that ridiculous1 questions Shall not be put to them. As far as railway mail clerks are concerned if, having had the opportunity of taking two examinations in one year, they are not able to paisa one such examination, they are not qualified to be railway mail clerks, because that examination is not a difficult one, but _ it proves whether they have the requisite knowledge to fill the office.

I hope the minister does not contemplate the abolishing all tests of educational accomplishments. I do not think you could fairly restrict the examination to what are the routine and practical duties of the railway mail clerk. There must be some educational standard that a man must reach before he can be appointed.
There is no question about that.

I agree with the minister that, in the past the papers set for 'Candidates entering this particular branch of the service have been unduly severe. At the same time I trust he will maintain an educational standard of some kind.

Certainly. What I meant was that the examination to be undergone should bear some relation to the work which the candidate has to perform. Of course the educational attainments must bear some relation to the work. However, it is not necessary for a sorter or stamper in the post office to possess the same degree of education as a man whose duties would require him to engage in correspondence and write letters in proper language. There should be some sort of a sliding scale by which the 'examinations will be based on the importahee of the work the man is going to do. That will be one of the difficulties in extending the control of the Civil Service Commission to the outside service. A proper sense of proportion must be maintained in order to make the idea practicable, but I hope that we will be able to realize the object which the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Le-mieux), and I think everybody in this House, has in view.
There is no question but that some years ago people were quite
What kind of examinations?

They are called case examinations. Every year an inspector goes through the various offices and cars and subjects the railway mail clerks to examination in order to see that they are well trained, and that they maintain their efficiency. But I quite agree with the Postmaster General, and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr .Macdonald) that the educational test for the railway mail clerk is too high. Why, with all due respect to the railway mail clerks, who are good officials and good men-we have heard in this House tc-day the maiden speech of a gentleman who tells us that he began life as a railway mail clerk, an excellent speech, indicating that the hon. gentleman will be quite an addition to this House, but I am sure that he will also admit what I say-it is 'lowering the standard of university and Royal Military College examinations to say that one who has passed those examinations may be admitted to the service.

Are the examinations which these men must pass the qualifying or the preliminary?
Mr. PELLETIER, Both. That is what I would call the absurdity of the present law. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) knows that we cannot keep up our staff of railway mail clerks strictly under the law. We have to take them on here and there under any name, 'labourers' for instance. Once we have engaged them, we take them into the service.

In my time railway mail clerks west of Lake Superior were entitled to an additional fifteen per cent on their salaries as a special allowance, because of the greater cost of living in the west. I suppose that is being maintained under this legislation?
All through this legislation, we have to take care of the extra cost of living in the west, which is admitted on all hands.
Is a knowledge of French necessary to qualify a railway mail clerk in the west?

If we exacted that in all cases, we could not find employees. We have to strain a point; we have to be liberal. In principle it is all right, but in practice, we have to do the best we can. In the west we have great difficulty in finding people to enter the service. In the east, on the contrary, men are anxious to enter. We must constantly send people from the east to the west to maintain our staff there. The cost of living in the west, as is well known, is very high; also the people there seem to make more money than they do here-in spite of the many

complaints we hear in the House about losses suffered, everybody seems to be prosperous in the west. I hope that this Bill will enable us to find in the west men who are to work in the west.

My hon. friend is quite right when he says that the Postmaster General is not obliged to demand of a candidate that he shall be qualified in both languages. Of course, it is of great advantage to a man to have both languages. But the examinations, by law and the constitution of the country, -may be passed in either language. If a candidate goes before the Civil Service Commission for the inside service, ihe may pass the examination in either French or English. But in this country no man has the same chance of succeeding, unless he speaks, writes and understands both languages. I cannot repeat too often to my English-speaking friends^and I say it with all candour-that the young French Canadian who speaks, writes and understands English as well as French, has two or three chances to one a3 against his young English-speaking competitor who has command of only one language. Besides in travelling all over the world my hon. friend will find that it is very important to know French.

I was going to object to that clause making an exception of the Royal Military College and universities, only that the Postmaster General says he is going to look into the question. The people in Ontario think that anybody who has passed through the military college and the universities is good enough for any place in the gift of this government, and surely their certificates are quite good enough to qualify a student for almost any business position in this country.

I think the minister should, at an early date, revise this whole system of examination. So much has been said as to what are the real duties of railway mail clerks, that one need not go over it again. At present the Civil Service Commission, under the head of ' History,' puts such questions as these to applicants:
Wliat do we owe to the following:-Magna Charts, Habeas Corpus, Wilberforoe, and Florence Nightingale-
Who was Jeanne Dare (Joan of Arc) ?
What was the Reign of Terror in France? What brought it about? Name the leading men who figured in it.
Sketch the career of William Lyon Mackenzie in the rebellion of 1837.
Fancy asking a young man going into the railway mail service such questions as these. If they were asked something about the career of William Lyon Mackenzie King, it might have been reasonable. Then here is another lot:
Give the plural of poet-laureate, crisis, madam, sheep and buffalo.
What I think should be required of a mail clerk is that he should be a fairly good writer, be able to do easy sums in arithmetic, and particularly be conversant with the geography of this country, of all the provinces in the Dominion; and to have more than a superficial knowledge of the geography of the United States. So far as European countries are concerned, the mail matter as a rule will go over direct to London, and there be sorted out. I hope the minister will cut out these examinations.
On subsection 6,
What is the meaning of that word ' university ' ? Will that cover our classical colleges?
Yes.

I think in Quebec there are 17 or 18 classical colleges affiliated to Laval University, and students who have completed their full course receive degrees, some the degree of Master of Arts, and others the degree of Bachelor of Arts. I would like to know from the hon. gentle man if the word 'university' will include such colleges?
Yes.

I would like to ask the minister what is the regulation by which the mileage apportioned to railway mail clerks is governed, that is, is there any uniformity in the mileage? There are perhaps five or six hundred clerks, and there must be great difference in the length of the routes. Is there any attempt at uniformity in the length of the routes, and the number of miles which each clerk has to travel? Otherwise, I can see that there might be some injustice in the payment of mileage. For instance, a man starting from Halifax and running to Montreal, would have a very long mileage; and I understand it is the same clerk or the same set of clerks who run up to Montreal, and turn to come back the next day. They would have a very long mileage, and consequently a very large pay; whereas a clerk running out of Halifax to Yarmouth, for instance, would have a short run, and 'short pay. Then again, the run from Halifax to Sydney is comparatively short, as compared with that from Halifax to Montreal. Is there some way by which the clerks are shifted about so that they may be treated with equality in the length of their runs and in the consequent amount of their payment? There are complaints in the service on this ground, possibly they have not reached the ears of the minister-eom-plaints against superintendents, because- I would not like to say it-they put their

favourites on good routes, and men who are not their favourites, on poor routes. I would like to see this work put on some basis, put under some independent supervision, so that all mail clerks should be treated on a par, so far as mileage and payment is concerned.

I think the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) is quite right. I may say that I have not, during the short time I have been at the head of the department, heard of any complaints in that respect. The hon. gentleman says there are complaints; if so, they have; not reached the head of the department. If any complaints come to my knowledge, they shall be dealt with in such a manner that all shall be treated fairly and justly. Of course the 'department ha3 to trust the railway mail superintendents, they are supposed to give each man a fair share of the mileage. I may say-so that it may go down on ' Hansard '-that it win be the aim of the department to treat all the railway mail clerks justly and fairly, so that each member of the staff shall receive a fair proportion of the mileage, and of the payment therefor. If any complaints are made to the head of the department they shall be heard. As a rule, I understand that the railway mail superintendents are doing this business in a fair manner. Of course there may be some difficulty in respect to long distances as compared with shorter runs. For instance, between Montreal and Ottawa, a railway mail clerk may travel as far as Vankleek Hill, and then double back to Montreal, and be with his family the same evening. Such arrangements exist in a certain number of cases. Others would prefer to go all the way from Montreal to Ottawa or vice versa. I understand that as far as is consistent with the interests of the service, the wishes of the clerks are taken into consideration bv the superintendent. if *complaints of the kind referred to reach me, I shall see that justice is done.
Mr, BENNETT (Simcoe). The inside' service at Ottawa stands on a different basis from the railway mail clerks. Railway mail clerks are, of necessity, all males, while in the inside service in Ottawa a lot of young women are employed. It is all very well to go wild on civil service examinations, but there must be limits. Whoever heard of a large steamship company with a line of ocean steamers asking for a competitive examination before appointing a captain? They select men according to their fitness. I know of no reason why a young man passing the ordinary preliminary examination, and in accord with the government of the day should not have preference in appointment. It is all very well for the hon. members for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and Rouville (Mr. Mr. McKENZIE.
Lemieux), those twin darlings of buncombe on all occasions, who stand up and claim entrance to the service for Grit and Tory alike. They have been singularly quiet on that subject for the last 15 years. It may be that they are now fatigued by their efforts, and worn out by the work they have done for their friends, they! now want them to be admitted to office by competitive examination. I want to place myself on record as being opposed to the appointment by the commission of railway mail clerks.

We have not only advocated equality in the appointment of civil servants, but we introduced legislation to provide for it and in the inside service ali parties have an equal chance, irrespective of politics. I ask my hon. friend if he does not think that in this way you secure a better service than by making selections from one party only. Is he of opinion that, after all, the appointment of a man in the outside service, a customs officer, or an excise man, or a letter carrier is of great political assistance to a member? There is an old adage in our province that when you appoint a man he becomes ungrateful, and you make 99 other people dissatisfied. Let it be under one commission, and let applications come from all parts and all sections or the community. Let the civil service be a national institution, not an institution in the hands of one party; let it be for the whole country.
Do I understand that this amendment gives a minister power to make permanent those temporary clerks now in the service no matter what their age may be?
Irrespective of age, the age limit is struck out, I think it is ridiculous.

Is the rumour true! which I heard in Montreal, that the old railway mail clerks who have attained the maximum of their salary, and are entitled to their superannuation, will get a superannuation equal to their salary?

I have never considered this question at all, it has never been presented to me.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 76) to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act-Mr. Cochrane.

When this Bill was under
consideration on Thursday there was some

criticism by hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to the cost of the railway, and they insinuated that it was owing to improper wastefulness and want of capacity on the part of the commissioners that it was costing so large an amount. The statement presented by the Minister of Railways shows that tihe total amount chargeable to capitall account is $187,781,128. That is the total amount which will be chargeable when the road is completed. Of that amount the total liability of the government is the interest on the actual expenditure of $187,781,128 for 7 years, which comes to $39,434,031. Then there is an estimate for betterments to the road during the 7 years it is operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific without interest of $7,884,840, and the interest on this is. estimated at $900,000, making a total of $48,218,871. I am not quite sure how the Minister of Railways and Canals comes to place the amount to be thus spent for betterments, but I presume that he has some reason for doing so. I should think that amount of betterments, $7,884,840, ought to be charged to capital account as is the case with other railways, or, if it is intended as the loss on the operation for seven years it should be charged to the government.
Under the agreement the betterment must be made by the government for fifty years.

With that explanation 1 repeat that the total amount of liability imposed upon the government in respect to the construction of the present Transcontinental railway will be $48,218,871. That is of course assuming that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will continue to operate the road after the period of seven years and pay the interest they are obliged to pay under the agreement. The statement made by the Minister of Railways included a charge for interest for the first three years after the road is taken over by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and assuming that there is not sufficient earned by the road during these three years to pay this interest, it would be chargeable to capital account, it, therefore, cannot fairly be stated that that would increase the liability of the government in respect to the expenses of building the railway. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) stated that figuring on the statement submitted to the committee by the Minister of Railways, $60,000,000 interest is going to be paid out by the country in connection with the road, instead of the $13,000,000 which we were told would be the cost by the then Prime Minister Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his Finance Minister, Mr. Fielding. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) then
estimates that the total liability for interest of the country in respect to the construction of this railway will be $60,000,000, and I venture to say that there is no hon. gentleman who will be disposed to believe that the hon. member (Mr. Ames) is in any way disposed to reduce the amount of liability which the .country will be under in this respect. Now, $60,000,000 is hot a very considerable amount of money when we take into consideration the immensity of the project, when nine years ago the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier undertook the construction of this railway. It is true that the cost of this road to the country will exceed the estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. rentleman sure that the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) mentioned $60,000,000 as the cost of the construction of this road?

No. He stated that that amount would have to be paid by the government for interest in respect of this undertaking. The government is not pay-;ng for the cost of the road as I understand. The Grand Trunk Pacific are ultimately to pay the cost of the road, either by actually purchasing it or by paying a rental which is estimated to amount to 'hree per cent, on the actual cost.
At what page of 1 Hansard 5 will I find the statement made by Mr. Ames?

At pages 3197-98. It has been asserted time and again that when the Bill was first before parliament, Mr. Fielding, then Finance Minister, stated that in his judgment the total amount for interest chargeable to the government, would be $13,000,000. I have heard that alleged statement denied by Mr. Fielding on the floor of the House, and I know that on a subsequent occasion the statement was made that $51,000,000 would cover the liability for interest incurred by the government in respect of the construction of this railway. Therefore, the amount of interest estimated by the late Minister of Finance and the amount which the hon. member (Mr. Ames) says the government will be liable for, do not disagree very much, there being a difference of $9,000,000 in the estimates of the two hon. gentlemen. Now, in the construction of every great undertaking it is not an uncommon thing that the actual expenditure should exceed the estimates. During the last forty years nearly every public work constructed by the government of this country has cost more money than it was estimated it would cost. In the construction of these very parliament buildings which was undertaken by the provinces of Ontario and Quebec in 1869, it was estimated that they would cost $2,000,000, but

when the buildings were completed it was found that they had cost $9,000,000, a difference of $7,000,000 above the estimate. In the case of the construction of the Panama canal, which was undertaken by the United States government, the actual experience of the work has proven that the estimate of the cost will be exceeded by an immense sum. I think the first estimate of the cost of the Panama canal by the officials who were charged to prepare that estimate, was $100,000,000 but, as an actual fact, the canal will cost $325,000,000 before the work is completed. There are reasons why the expenditure on the Transcontinental railway has largely exceeded the estimate, quite apart from any suggestion that there was want of capacity on the part of the Transcontinental Railway Commission. Take, for instance, that section of the railway be-twen Moncton and .Chipman; I understand that in the original specifications drawn by the engineers in charge of the work it was stated that for the first fifty miles west of Moncton there was no rock, and that common earth excavation would be the material met with, but, when they came to build the road it was found that this first fifty miles west of Moncton was almost exclusively solid rock. That mistake would seem to reflect to some extent upon the capacity of the engineers who were entrusted with the preparation of the specification in respect to that section. I suppose they could have made a more correct estimate of the cost of construction if they had gone to the expense of sinking test pits, from Moncton to Winnipeg. They would then be in a position to state with greater accuracy what was the nature of the excavations which would have to he done. But, after having sunk these test pits, which would have cost millions of dollars, how much better off would the country he in respect of the knowledge thereby gained? If those who are disposed to criticise the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners are able to prove that they have been guilty of any incapacity or want of integrity in relation to the work which had been entrusted to them, then, of course, it would be a most serious reflection upon them.
But the reason why the cost of the eastern section exceeded the estimate, was because, instead of common excavation, there was solid rock. If test pits had been made in order to enable the engineers to make an absolutely correct report upon the conditions, tlie country would not have benefited to the extent of a dollar, but rather would have lost the cost of making these test pits. Whatever the nature of the excavation was, it had to be done once the construction of the Transcontinental railway was entered upon, by virtue of legislation, empowering the government to carry on that work. I am going to cite another Mr. KYTE.
case-the construction of the railway in the neighbourhood of La Tuque. I understand that when the specifications for that section were being prepared, the engineers thought that owing to the greatly increased cost of constructing the road with a grade of 4-10ths of one per cent., a grade of 1 per cent, might be reasonably satisfactory in that locality. The Grand Trunk Pacific company, however, insisted upon the 4-10ths giade being adhered to, and the consequence was, that a change from 1 per cent, to 4-10ths of 1 per cent, in the neighbour-hod of La Tuque, for the distance of a mile, added to the cost of the Transcontinental railway to the extent of $1,250,000.
Does the hon. gentleman state that there is a 4-10ths grade between Moncton and Quebec?

With the exception of a couple of pusher grades, I believe it is a 4-10ths grade. Now, the National Transcontinental railway is not the first great railway undertaken in this country. Some 30 years ago, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company undertook to build a railway across the continent. This is a company which was organized for the purpose of building the railway as a private undertaking; and, except for the grants of money end land and other concessions made to the company by the then Conservative government, the obligation to finance the scheme, was entirely in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company itself. That company received from the la^e Conservative government: in cash, $25,000,000; in railways completed and uncompleted, $65,000,000; and 25,000,000 acres of land, estimated to be worth $144,216,624; a total Of $234,216,624 to assist them in carrying out their undertaking. Now, that is an enormous sum of money for the government of this country 30 years ago to bestow upon a company which only undertook to do in respect of a transcontinental railway system that which -was undertaken by the government led by the right hon. the leader of the opposition, a few years ago. Of that sum, which the late Conservative government contributed to assist the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, not one dollar came back to the people of this country, and the government does not to-day receive one dollar of interest from that expenditure. Hon. gentlemen opposite, who criticise with such unmeasured language, the extravagance of the late Liberal government in carrying on the construction of the Transcontinental railway, have -strongly commended the wisdom and the statesmanship of the government led by tire late Sir John A. Macdonald in making that contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Therefore, if the sum of $234,216,624 was only a reasonable assistance to give to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at &

time when labour was cheap, when supplies were cheap, when the cost of living was very much less than it is to-day, I fail to see why these hon. gentlemen should criticise and condemn the late Liberal government for contributing $60,000,000 towards the construction of another transcontinental railway, which, in the judgment^ of all the people in Canada is absolutely necessary to keep up with the present development of this country. In the statement which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals presented to the House the other night, he said that the Transcontinental railway had cost up to the present $113,853,300, and that it is estimated that to complete the road it will be necessary to spend $57,872,700 more. Now, according to the statements which have been submitted to the House from time to time, it is estimated that two-thirds of the whole undertaking is completed at tire present time. Therefore, only one-third of the work remains to be done; 'and, if the figures submitted by the minister are correct, it would appear that it is going to cost the country nearly $1,000,000 more proportionately to complete the one-third of the road than it cost to complete the two-thirds that is now finished.

The hon. gentleman does not mean that 'to he a fair statement, because he knows that the most expensive part of any road is the terminals and the right of way, which in this case are not yet paid for.
The cost of the land for terminals is largely included in the amount thus far expended, as stated by the Minister of Railways the other evening.
The hon. gentleman cannot prove that statement. He made the statement, as I understood him, that the right of way has been paid for. Now let him prove that.

I am stating that two-thirds of the road has been completed up to the present time, that one-third of it remains to be completed, and that this one-third according to the figures submitted by the hon. minister, wild cost proportionately $1,000,000 more than the two-thirds of the [DOT] road now completed. Therefore, notwithstanding the excuse given by hon. gentlemen opposite for terminating the services of the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners that owing to their incapacity and want of experience they 'allowed the road vo cost too much, the future work to be done under the management of Mr. Leonard, the present chairman of the board; notwithstanding the contention that this change is made on the ground of economy, the one-third of the road still to be done will cost $1,000,000 more in proportion than what has been thus la.' completed.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the argument that this change is to be made in the interest of economy and in order to keep down the cost of the Transcontinental railway, in so far as it is not completed at the present time is scarcely borne out by the facts. Another criticism directed against the board is that they are not railway builders. Hon. gentlemen , supporting the present government have questioned the wisdom of the late Premier because, in selecting the members of the Transcontinental Commission he failed to choose men with proper qualifications. It was suggested that instead of merchants, lawyers and business men generally, the right hon. gentleman should have chosen engineers to carry on this undertaking. I have before me the list of the first directors of the 'Canadian Pacific railway who were entrusted with carrying out the construction of that undertaking some thirty years ago, and in that list I fail to find the name of a single engineer whose judgment and experience seemed to be necessary in order to assist the directors in executing their task in the most business-like and most economical manner. The following are the gentlemen to whom I allude:
George Stephen, Montreal, merchant; Duncan McIntyre, Montreal, merohant; John S. Kennedy, New York, banker; R, B. Angus, St. Paul, Esquire; James J. Hill, St. Paul, Esquire; Henry Stafford Northcote, London, Esquire; Pascal Dr. P. Grenfell, London, merchant; Charles Day Rose, London, merchant; Baron J. de Reinach, Paris, hanker.
Now there is not a single engineer in the whole of that list of the original directors of the Canadian Pacific railway. They were business men, they were merchants and bankers, they were men who were accustomed to do business according to the methods in which business was understood in those days but they had had no experience in railway building. When they required technical knowledge or technical assistance, they went to engineers whose services they engaged for that particular purpose. Therefore, the wisdom of the late government is not to be questioned because they did not appoint engineers on the board of the Transcontinental Railway Commission. The Act which constituted that board gave them power to employ the services of engineers for the purposes of the undertaking and that is what was done. Now Mr. Leonard the present chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Board, attended a banquet in the city of Brantford on the 3rd of January last and in responding to a toast there took occasion to refer to the character of the work of the Transcontinental railway that was done by the present commission. Sir, when I

hear hon. gentlemen criticising the manner in which this railway has been built, the manner in which the work was carried on, I am inclined to think that Mr. Leonard's .speech at the banquet in question is a very excellent reply. Mr. Leonard says:
What the cost will be to complete the road to iMoncton is hard to say, but it is now nearly all under construction, all but 400 to 500 miles between Cochrane and Winnipeg. The Quebec 'bridge which, when finished, will be the largest bridge in the world, will take 48,000 tons of steel, and will take five or six years to build. Going east our line runs at about 4-10 grade, and an engine will haul 1,600 tons, whereas on other roads where a 1 per cent grade exists, 800 is all that can he hauled.	.
' The Transcontinental/ he declared, is being built in the best and most durable manner known. It is also of great military advantage, giving Canada an unlimited width, in' spite of the millions that will be spent in its construction.	,
The National Transcontinental is a national asset, not a burden to the people of Canada. Our enormous grain and mineral wealth goes to show what a truly wonderful Country we have, and we should all do our best to make it a strong link in the empire's drain.
Mr. Chairman, that is a certificate of which both the Transcontinental Railway Commission and the late government might very justly be proud. Mr. Leonard has referred to the character of the work that was carried on, and the excellent character of the railway in respect to its carrying capacity as compared with other railways. I need not remind you, Mr. Chairman, that an enormous proportion of the cost incurred in the construction of this railway was due to the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the government of Canada as well, came to the conclusion that they should have a better railway than any transcontinental line existing at the present time. They desire a railway whose carrying capacity will exceed that of any railway at present engaged in transporting the products of western Canada to the maritime provinces and vice versa. In order to do that it was necessary to build a very much more expensive road, but they were amply justified in expending the additional amount of money when we take into account the enormous saving in operating expenses pointed out by Mr. Leonard as compared with similar expenses on the other transcontinental railways. I think that in discussing the liability of the late government and the responsibility of the present commission for the large amount of money which this railway has cost, we must not fail to take into account the circumstance that the whole liability imposed upon the government in regard to the construction of this road, not including the Quebec bridge, is Mr. KTTE.
$60,000,000 if we take the statement of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). Compared with that there is the sum of $234,216,224 incurred by the government of Canada and the people of this country for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. When the transcontinental line is completed it will yield a revenue to the government of Canada equal to three per cent on every dollar that it cost in its construction, and in default of the payment of that rental by the Grand Trunk Pacific it will become the property of the people, whereas the Canadian Pacific railway upon which this large amount of public money was spent in the form of subsidies and subventions which I have referred to, yields not one dollar of interest to the people of Canada, but the whole advantage of this enormous expense has accrued to a private corporation. I have no reflection to make upon the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but if it was wisdom on the part of the late Conservative government to assist the Canadian Pacific railway to the extent they did from the public funds, surely it does not indicate a lack of statesmanship for the late Liberal government to build another transcontinental railway at a cost of little more than one fourth of the amount whidh the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway entailed on the people of Canada.

It seems to me that this matter has not so far received the consideration which should be given to an important question of this kind.
This matter is not to be regarded from a sectional standpoint but from the standpoint of the whole Dominion. I believe that the people of this Dominion approve of the form of organization under which this great national work was undertaken and under which it has been so efficiently carried on, and that sufficient reasons have not been given for the change that is proposed.

The other day, when we were discussing the reduction of the number of these commissioners, my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) spoke of the cost of building the Transcontinental railway, and gave that as the reason why these commissioners should be removed from office. I was a little surprised to hear him take up the case in the way he did. It seemed to me a partisan discussion, and I am always surprised to hear a business man discuss a business question from a partisan standpoint.
I was asked for a statement, and I gave it. That's all.

I was not speaking of the minister (Mr. Cochrane), but of the

hon. member for St. Antoine. I have no fault to find with the statement of the minister. We asked him for facts, and he gave them. At least, I assume that-
They were on the authority of your own engineer.

Quite so. I have no fault to find with the statement of the hon. minister, but I was surprised, as I have said, at the hon. member for St. Antoine discussing this from a partisan standpoint. Now, I do not pretend to know much about the building of railways, but I have asked many people who do know about the building of railways, as to the quality of this railway which is now approaching completion, and I have been told by one and all who have seen the road that it is finished in a first class manner. We all know that it is quite the custom for railways in this country and in the United States to be built at first in a temporary manner-first get the rails down in any old way, and then go on and finish up the road. Those of us who have read the evidence before the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States on the question of freight rates, know that the capital expenditure on the transcon-tental railways in the United States has been enormous-I believe quite as much as stated by my hon. friend from St. Antoine when he said that this road would cost $130,000 a mile. I believe there is not a road through a similar country in the United States which has been built and put in reasonably permanent condition at a less cost than $130,000 a mile. I believe also that if the road is finished in the way capable men say that it is being finished at a cost of $130,000 a mile it is a reasonable figure, considering the portion of country through which it runs and the vast necessary expense, in getting in supplies. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was attacked the other day on the ground that this railway went through the section of country that it does. I believe that in a very short time it will be proven that this was cne of the wisest steps that could possibly have been taken in the interest of the country at large. This is one of the sections of the country of which we knew little. It will open up a new region and will practically extend the boundaries of this country very largely. I believe that when the road is running you will find that it will pay from the first day so far as traffic is concerned. Local traffic will probably develop in that country never dreamed of, possibly, by the people of Ontario, before this road went through. I repeat but with all due deference to my hon. friend that I believe the road will pay from the time it is built. Also I think most emphatically that considering, as I said, the
country through which it is built, it will be found on investigation, and a commission has been appointed to investigate- that the road has cost no more than it should have cost in view of the difficulties that had to be overcome in con; struction. And I, for one would not vote to-day to have it built in any other way so far as thoroughness is concerned,, nor would I vote to have it built through a different section of country. It has been argued here that it should have been built to North Bay, and then via the old Northern to Toronto and by a connection to Montreal. Nobody would think of carrying heavy freight that way.
However, it may be said that this has nothing to do with the question before us. As to the commissioners, I believe in the old adage ' two heads are better than one, even if one is a cabbage head/ 1 believe that the. probabilities are that for the remainder of this undertaking it would be better to leave the commission as it is. But the minister has seen fit to do otherwise. If he can save the expense of the extra commissioners and do the work as well, that will be all right. I do-not know the head of the commission. They say he is a capable man. He would need to be a capable man to be as good as four other men. For my part, 1 am a great believer in a number of counsellors where great undertakings are to be considered.

I would like to point cut also that I think it is unfair for any hen. member to attack the expenditure without taking into consideration the quality of the work done. We all know that a man could build a warehouse 60 feet x 100 feet by using galvanized sheets of iron and rough lumber for between $2,500 and $3,000; by improving the

That is not the criticism as I understood it However, if my hon. friend so understood it, that is his privilege. Our present opposition, it appears to me, are in somewhat of an apologetic mood about something. What is that something if it is not the tremen-Mr. NESBITT.
dous cost in excess of the estimates that were placed before this House in 1903 in regard to this National Transcontinental railway. Those of us who were in the House in 1903 remember clearly what was said about it at that time. I have before me a document which hon. members opposite will likely recognize: it is a speech of the right hon. the" leader of the opposition who was then Prime Minister, and I wish to read one or two extracts from that speech to show what he said about it at that time, and he said it so well, in the opinion of his followers, that they thought it wise to make a campaign sheet of it, and it was spread broadcast throughout the country in the election campaign subsequent to the session of 1904. Let me read a few words which fell from the lips of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition to-day, in respect to the cost of the National Transcontinental railway.
So that here again the whole of the liability which is incurred by the government for the building of that section from Moncton to Winnipeg is simply seven years of interest. The sum total of the money to he paid by the government for the construction of that line of railway from Moncton to the Pacific Ocean will be in the neighborhood of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000, and not a cent more.
I have never heard the right hon. gentleman explain clearly what he meant by those words, and I have never heard any one of his followers since explain to us what he meant when he made that statement.
We know that he could not have meant that the road would cost $12,000,000 or $13,000,000, that it was an interest charge to which he referred. But we have an estimate from the Minister of Finance of that day, Mr. Fielding, in respect to the cost of this National Transcontinental railway, and I shall take the figures which Mr. Fielding gave us at that time as being the figures which the late government authorized. The figures which Mr. Fielding gave us in the year 1903, in debate in this House were these:	The railway from
Moncton to Winnipeg would cost $54,609,000, made up in this way, from Winnipeg to Quebec at $28,000 a mile, $41,300,000; from Quebec to Moncton at $25,000 per mile, $10,000,000, a total of $51,300,000. He added to that a certain amount of interest which brought his estimate up to $54,609,-
000.	In the following year, 1904, when the government came before parliament with a revised contract Mr. Fielding brought his estimate up to an average of something over $31,000 per mile, for this section of the National Transcontinental railway, and raised his total estimate to somewhere in the vicinity of $58,000,000. The government of that day went to the people of this country on these figures, and on

the figures cited by Sir Wilfrid Laurier of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000, and they received the endorsation of the people.
Now we have placed before us the figures which this road has cost up to date, and which it is likely to cost and I have no doubt these figures are correct. According to tihe figures given us by the hon. the Minister of Railways this part of the road will cost not $25,000 or $28,000, or $31,250, as Mr. Fielding estimated in 1904, but $130,800 per mile; not a total of $54,609,000 as Mr. Fielding estimated in this House, but of $236,000,000. These things should be considered by non. gentlemen opposite when they are discussing this subject, and I am not surprised to find them in an apologetic mood in regard to this expenditure. I look upon the construction of the National Transcontinental railway as one of the worst bungles of the late government, and it seems to me that the present government were amply justified in adopting another system of management of that great undertaking and changing the commission under whose direction this tremendous expenditure has been made.
What was the object in building this road? In 1900, 1901 and 1902, there was an agitation in this country in respect to getting the crops transported from the west to the seaboard, and to the markets of the world, and there was a desire on the part of the government of that day, as there is on the part of the government of this day, to facilitate in every way the transportation of the crops of the'northwest to the markets of the world. In 1902 the Grand Trunk people made an application to the late government in writing, and that document was laid on the table of this House in due course. It was an application for permission to build a road connecting with the Grand Trunk system at North Bay, Ontario, into the wheatfields of the northwest. They asked certain concessions from the government of the day, concessions which would, in my estimation, be very unimportant as compared with the tremendous cost of this railroad as we have it before us to-day. The right hon. gentleman who led the government of that day made some statements with regard to the necessity of doing something in order to allleviate the conditions existing in the northwest, On July 30, 1903, he sa:d in this House:
We consider that it is the duty of all those who sit within these walls by the will of the people, to provide immediate means whereby the products of those new settlers may find an exit to the ocean at the least possible cost, and whereby, likewise, a market may be found in this new region for those who toil in the forests, in the fields, in the mines, in the shops of the older provinces. Such is our duty; it is immediate and imperative. . .
To those who urge upon us the policy of to-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow; to those who tell us, Wait, wait, wait; to those who advise us to pause, to consider, to reflect, to calculate and to inquire, our answer is: No, this is not a time for deliberation, this is a time for action. The flood tide is upon us that leads on to fortune; if we let it pass it may never recur again. If we let it pass, the voyage of our national life, bright as it is to-day, will be bound in shallows. We cannot wait, because time does not wait.
Here was the situation in 1903, and I must say that the situation is not im-improved to-day. What has happened ? The Laurier government, instead of pursuing a business-like policy in regard to the building of this railway, delayed its construction in every possible way so that in 1912, nine years later, the people of the west have no better facilities for getting out their crops than they had in 1903. But what is more serious to my mind is that instead of the late government proceeding to complete that railroad from Winnipeg to Cochrane Junction where it connects with the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway which connects with the Grand Trunk system at North Bay, in order that these crops might be transported from the west and the people of the west might have relief as was forecasted by the statement of the Prime Minister of that day, what has happened ? The government have completed the railway from Quebec to Moncton but it may be three years before they are able to make connection between Winnipeg and Cochrane Junction, to connect with the Grand Trunk system in order that the crops may be brought out.
Thus there are two main grounds of complaint against the late government in connection with the building of this railway, first, the great extravagance which has been permitted in its construction and, second, the unreasonable delay in the construction of that part of the road which would afford much needed relief to the people of the northwest.

It is quite evident that the hon. member (Mr. Kemp), who is a sort of fo'castle member of the administration is somewhat behind the times owing to the fact that he was not here in the last parliament. The hon. gentleman does not seem, judging from his utterances, to realize the responsibility that rests upon him as a member of the government. He is worried over the fact that the government did not commence work at Lake Abitibi and branch off east and west, and he seems to have no idea about the conveniences required for getting in supplies and starting terminals and getting in the material necessary to carry on construction. He is such a great railway builder [DOT]



that he would not do anything that expert railway builders thought it wise to do. Then the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp), does not seem to be aware of the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific railway is in existence from Fort William to the city of Winnipeg, and that even to-day it brings the traffic of the west in touch with the other railway systems of the Dominion. The hon. member (Mr. Kemp), has followed the lead of the hon. member (Mr. Ames), in misrepresenting the right hon, Sir Wilfrid Laurier as saying, when he introduced the Bill, that $13,000,000 would be the amount of money the railway would cost this country. I am more surprised at the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp), indulging in such misrepresentations than I am at the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), because we all remember that that latter gentleman a few years ago travelled all over the country with lantern slides and talking of the restitution that was to take place the moment the Conservative party came into power. Well, the lantern slide has been put in the garret and the hon. member (Mr. Ames), is not bothering himself about restitution. The chief occupation of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) now seems to be to act as a bellwether to the Nationalist portion of the gentlemen with whom he is sitting on the government benches, endeavouring to lead them into camp, and to keep them there until they get through the Manitoba school question and other such things, and then of course he won't care much about the Nationalists. The hon. member from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), has given up the lantern slide show, and he comes here to start an extraneous discussion on this Bill and to resurrect old stories which were shown to be baseless time and again in former parliaments, as to the supposed cost of the Transcontinental railway. Now, Sir Wilfrid Laurier never meant to say that the Transcontinental railway was only going to cost the country thirteen millions, and as a matter of fact he never did say so, but these gentlemen want to put such a false interpretation upon the words of the late Prime Minister.
What interpretation did you put on these words?

My hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), is another gentleman who is sitting at the feet of the wrong Gamaliel. I set against their interpretation of the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier the opinion of the hon. member from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), who has studied the matter long and laboriously and who, with all respect, knows more about the matter than most gentlemen sitting on the government benches. Here Mr. MACDONALD.
is what the hon. member for South Simcoe said in the last parliament:
We, the members of the House understood that the Prime Minister did not mean that the total expenditure on the construction of the road would be $13,000,000; he intended to convey the proposition that the money that would be paid out and not received back was $13,000,000
That is not what your campaign literature said.

Does the hon. member from Manitoba (Mr. Bradbury) go back upon the statement of the man who was his leader in the past parliament in all matters connected with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway?
