The hon. member for South Simcoe has spent toilsome days and sleepless nights endeavouring to extract some campaign material for the benefit of his party out of the words of the former Prime Minister, and he was able to tell the House what the meaning of the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was and the hon. member from Manitoba (Mr. Bradbury) was not here in that parliament and he knows nothing about it. It is not common sense to suppose that the right hon. gentleman meant that the Transcontinental railway would be built for $13,000,000 because that would represent only $7,200 a mile, and everybody who knows anything, knows that it is impossible to build a single mile of railway anywhere in Canada for $7,200. Contemporaneously with the statement made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier was the estimate made not by Mr. Fielding, but by Mr. Schreiber, a gentleman of long experience, a gentleman who advised the Conservative government in connection with the_ construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, and he estimated that the railway would cost $62,000,000. But the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) was not deceived as to the cost of the railway, because he, with his great engineering knowledge, made an estimate all his own, and he said that the railway would cost the country $73,000,000.
Where is that in 'Hansard?'

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) will find it in 'Hansard,' and it would be well for him to look over his old speeches and get some new ideas from them. The genial gentleman who represented Lennox and Addington in the past parliament estimated the cost at $114,000,000; the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) entered into the realm of speculation, and he was not worrying about the $13,000,000, for he calculated that it would cost $100,000,000.
That was a nearer estimate than yours.
Including the right of way ?
Will the hon. gentleman answer a question?

No, I do not propose to answer any questions of my hon_ friend from Sirnooe. This committee know me well enough to know that I do not mind answering questions, and I have no personal objection to my hon. friend from Simcoe; but this question habit of his is becoming too much of a habit. We -are told this railway is going to cost something like $130,000 per mile. Now, let us see-just where we are. Mark you, Mr. Chairman, the expenditure which the late government were responsible for was the expenditure which was made down to the day they gave up their office. They are not responsible for the expenditure that hon. gentlemen opposite make. If the plans were wrong, change them; if the grades are too good and cost too much, if the curvatures which the late government desired to obtain cost too much, bon. gentlement opposite can remedy that. It is in their power; it has been in their power ever since they came into office in October, and will be in their power until this railway is completed. Let ns see what has been done. Taking my hon. friend'-s statement, we find that up to date 1,656 miles of main line track have been laid, -and the cost has been, $66,000 a mile. Grading has been done on 309 miles more. The situation, then, is that grading has been -done and rails have-been laid on 1,965 miles at a cost of $56,008-a mile. That is what the -late government is responsible for, and -every dollar that has-been expended since that time and that will be expended in the future, my hon, friend the Minister of Railways will be responsible for. He knows that the contracts which have been let are not contracts which bind the government to h-ave-the road built on any gradient. The contractors are paid so much a yard for the earth removed, and my -hon. friend can send his engineers out to tell them to dispense with a grade of 4/10ths of 1 per cent,

to dispense with the features which we had been providing for, and instead of putting in concrete and stone foundations to their bridges, to put in wooden structures; and instead of having iron bridges upon these -structures, to dispense with them and put in wooden 'bridges and put the power in the 'hands of my hon. friend "the Minister of Railways to do it. And let me tell you that if from this hour the cost per mile of this railway exceeds the figures which I am giving to-night, the responsibility will rest upon the hon. gentleman whom he appointed. Let there be no mistake about that. My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) laughs. He has a very curious idea about his position. I wonder what kind of a Minister of Railways he thinks he [DOT]ought to be? I want to tell him that in *what he undertakes he is responsible to the people of this country and to parliament who have to vote the expenditure every year. When the hon. minister comes here and asks us to vote money he is responsible for the expenditure, and I say again if from this moment in the construction of the balance of this railway the expenditure of the past of the late commission is exceeded in any way, the hon. gentleman will be responsible for it.
Do you mean that the late government had reached the limit?

The hon. member from Peterborough is one of these singular *gentleman in regard to whom it is most difficult to tell where he is at or what he is driving at. What I say is this: That either my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) is complaining about the late government spending too much in the Transcontinental railway construction or he is not. If he is complaining that the railway has cost too much, the remedy is in the hands of himself and his friends, he can cheapen the cost of construction. He 'can lessen it in the way I have indicated. Now,, I have pointed out that the cost of constructing the railway that has so far been built is $56,000 a mile. To complete the balance of 426 miles it is estimated by my bon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) and I have taken these figures from his statement in order to show the House and the country what a peculiar position of affairs it is- that although it cost the late government only $56,000 a mile to build what they had built, he proposes to estimate the cost of the remainder at $94,000 a mile. In other words, although these gentlemen who are sitting on the right of the Speaker have been talking day in and day out ever since this railway enterprise was initiated, about the tremendous cost to Canada of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the National Transcontinental railway, and that the late government had completed two-thirds of the Mr. MACDONALD.
railway at a cost of $56,000 a mile, when they come to this House to 'tell us what they are going to do in future they estimate the cost at $94,000 a mile. Those figures are simply taken from the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) and if he wants to exclude the cost of terminals and shops-
Which they had no authority to do.
Who had no authority to do so?
The government.

We will consider that in a moment. At present I am discussing with my hon. friend the question of costs, and .1 say if my hon. friend excludes from this statement the cost of the terminals and the cost of the shops-

Did I say that there was any such number of miles built? If I remember aright there was given in his statement so many miles of grading, and so many miles of track laid. That does not finish a road, and the hon. gentleman knows it if he knows anything about building a railway. What about the ballasting?
My hon. friend says that does not finish the road. It goes a iong way to finish the road. I am taking his own figures.
Then take them in the right way.
My hon. friend wants to deceive the House when he brings figures here and tells us-
Order.

My hon. friends opposite are getting very sensitive. The minister brings before this House a statement and here" it is: ' Length of the line from Moncton to Winnipeg 1,804-7 miles. Grading completed 1,587 miles, or 76-82 per cent of the whole. Then track laid 1,378-7.'
The track cost something.
' Main line and in addition 278-7 miles in siding.' Track laid certainly advanced construction.
The rails cost something.
' Telegraph line 9,982 miles, bridges 82-75 per cent '.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How many miles?

Nine hundred and eighty-two. I beg my hon. friend's pardon, it could not, of course, be 9,000. Now, here is the point: I say if we take the figures contained in the statement prepared and submitted to the House by the Minister of

Railways, and if we exclude the cost of terminals and shops from the estimates of the future cost of the road it still means that the minister to-day contemplates spending $85,000 a mile to build the balance of the road when it only cost the late government $56,000 a mile for the railway built by them. Here is a splendid opportunity for these hon. gentlemen to put into practice all their theories about railway construction. They expressed the belief that the late government did not know how to build railroads and they were not going to get a lot of lawyers and put them on the Transcontinental Railway Commission.
Hear, hear.

When the government wanted somebody to investigate the late Transcontinental Railway Commission who do you suppose they appointed as chairman? They went to Hamilton and secured my very pleasant friend, Mr. Lynch Staunton, a good lawyer, who year in and year out, is the legal adviser of the Ontario government.
That is why they get along so well.

My hon friends will find that the Ontario government is not getting on so well some of these days. Well they have appointed Mr. Lynch Staunton as chairman of this commission of investigation, a gentleman who never had anything to do with a railway in his life, whose specialty is water-powers, and whose occupation has been confined solely to matters of that kind. The late government appointed as the first chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, Mr. Wade, a distinguished lawyer, who had connection with railway corporations in the province of Nova Scotia, who had not only engaged in the operation of railways himself, but helped to build them. He was succeeded by Mr. Parent, who had executive and business ability of the highest character, who had been Prime Minister of the province, and whose judgment as a business man is recognized by men of all classes in the province of Quebec, English and French, wherever he is known.
Did lie not have something to do with the Quebec bridge affair? What executive ability did he show there?
We will discuss the Quebec bridge matter at the proper time.
I do not think he showed much ability in the Quebec bridge matter.
Yes.
Mr. Gutelius is not connected with the construction of railways..
Yes.
He is connected with the maintenance which is entirely different from construction.
And construction too.
Where did he construct a railway in Canada?
He helped in the construction of the Central Ontario railwayline.

He was in charge of maintenance and my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) will find that his experience is not connected with railway construction. And if I am correctly informed the government could not find a man in Canada, who was engaged in railway construction and they had to take a man who was a citizen of the United States.
The head of the Grand Trunk railway is a citizen of the United States and you took him up.

My hon. friend is reverting to the old tu quoque argument which is about all flattened out. My hon. friend and his party have boasted of the ability with which they were to come in to-do everything so splendidly and properly. None of the mistakes of their predecessors were to be repeated, none of the errors into which they had fallen were to again occur.
My objection was not to the western part, but to the part running down to New Brunswick.

Well, that is interesting. My hon. friend did not want this eastern section of the road, he wanted it to come down to North Bay. He did not want to open up the hinterland of Ontario and Quebec, that was not his .
COMMONS *
ambition for Canada at all. He wanted to have a branch line down into the city of Toronto, and Canada and all her aspirations could have gone a begging if he got that. Then of course he was reckless as to whether traffic would Dass J own through the United States. If I recollect right, the hon. member for East Toronto was not one of those who are in lavour of a preference being given to Canadian ports. So my hon. friend's ambition for Canada would have been satisfied by a line running down from North Bay to Toronto, and the rest of Canada could go hang. But the men who were in charge of public affairs at that time had a greater ambition for Canada. They looked to this northern land, and they believed, what we all know at the present time, that from year to year the population would increase, and that that great country would steadily grow in importance. Why, my optimistic friend the Minister of the Interior, I am sure, would not agree with the hon. member for East Toronto, because he told us the other night that he was in favour, after you got the Hudson Bay railway down to Port Nelson or Fort Churchill of building another railway further north than the Grand Trunk Pacific, going down to Labrador, and having connection form there to England. So I say that all the evidence points to the .fact that we did not start a moment too soon. I had some doubts at one time as to the attitude of the leader of the government on this question, but in the discussion which we had in the House I think two years ago, he said he was not one of those who agreed with the member for East Toronto. I was glad to know that my right hon. friend at that time took the position that he was in favour of the construction of the road from Winnipeg to Quebec. Now we all entered upon that project. Almost every one in Canada came to the conclusion that this railway was a necessity, and everybody agrees to-day that it was not started a minute too soon. Look at the clamour that comes from that western land with 400,000,000 bushels of grain waiting for transport. My hon. friend from East Toronto who did not want this railway built to Quebec in 1903, complains to-day because it is not built fast enough. So I say the policy of the government in 1903 has been amply justified. Everybody in Canada at that time, and ever since, has taken it for granted that the National Transcontinental railway was a necessity, and has not been started a moment too soon. Yet here to-day, when hon. gentlemen get into power, they proceed to change this commission and dismiss three of the commissioners, and they propose to run this whole thing with one commissioner. They start in a peculiar manner with regard to it. After they have decided Mr. MACDONALD. "
upon doing away with three commissioners, they proceed in an illegal way to appoint an assistant chairman.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When was he appointed vice-chairman?

I am speaking of the statement made by the Minister of Railways. He said:
The lion. ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Em-merson) wanted a copy of the order in council. I have a copy of it here. I may say that I find that there was a mistake in that, in the statement that it was recommended by the commission instead of by the chairman of the commission. But I took the matter up with the chairman, and he informed me that his law clerk had advised him that he had a right to do what he had done, and that the matter was brought before the commission, and Mr. Mclsaac, one of the commissioners, thought that he was acting within his jurisdiction in appointing Mr. Macpherson. I also wish to say that I was misinformed, and misinformed the House, when I said that Mr. Macpherson's salary had not been increased. I am informed that it has been increased.
What is Mr. Macpherson's salary at the present time?
What was it before?

$5,000, I think.
The result is the expression ' vice-chairman ' was used by the minister.
Oh no, I said assistant to the chairman.

If that gives any satisfaction to the minister he is welcome to it. There is no power to appoint an assistant to the chief commissioner. There are four commissioners, this Bill proposes to wipe them out and make just one commissioner. It does not say anything about an assistant chairman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It does not say assistant chairman.

Assistant to the chairman. If there is to be an assistant to the chairman he should be appointed by the commission, clearly so under the law and the commission have not appointed him. But in some way or other the Minister of Railways, who is going to economize and build the railway more cheaply, at the very inception takes a subordinate from under the chief engineer, appoints him assistant to the chairman, and gives him $2,500 more than before, when under the law he has no right to do so. I warn the minister that he will not go very far until he finds some of the acute critics who are versed in all these matters in connection with National Transcontinental railway expenditures, and who sit not far from him, will find that he is inaugurating an expenditure which he has no justification for making. The result of the action of the minister is that instead of doing away with the four commissioners he will still have two commissioners, as he is giving the assistant to the chairman the salary of one of the old commissioners. The minister has acted entirely without warrant or authority.
A word or two in regard to my hon. friend's estimate. Hon. gentlemen will notice that the minister has made some curious estimates here. He says that 72-86 per cent of the whole road is completed. He says that there has already, been expended $7,681,700, in engineering expenses. That means that all the location surveys, the preliminary surveys from end to end of the country have been made, and that you have 76 per cent of the road constructed; and yet my hon. friend proposes to spend $3,850,000 more in surveys. How does he work that out in proportion? I have not made an estimate, but any gentleman can figure the proportion.
Engineering and expenses' up to date, are set down at $7,681,700, and the minister says that he contemplated this charge will amount lo $3,850,000 more, so that I should think some details of that ought to be given.
Well, that is the statement signed by the engineer.

Well, the minister is responsible and not the engineer and it is the minister who should give the information to this House, by which it may be guided. The minister comes to this House asking us to pass legislation on the basis of certain information he has given, and I say that it is for him to give us some explanation of that exorbitant estimate of $3,800,000 for engineering expenses yet to be incurred. Now, under ' headquarters, salaries and expenses,' the total expense to date since the initiation of the work, is given at $1,732,900, and notwithstanding that only twenty-four per

cent of the road remains to be completed, we are told that the expenses of the headquarters staff will amount to, for the future, $1,267,000. Surely we are entitled to some explanation as to how the minister and his engineers have arrived at that estimate. In the past, we have had four commissioners, and although the minister is dispensing with the services of three of them, and although, according to the rule of proportion, the expenses at headquarters should only be one-half million dollars for the balance of the road, the minister tells us that it will amount to $1,267,000. Surely parliament must have some explanation as to that. Then again, with seventy-six per cent, of the road completed, the minister gives us an estimate that it will cost $2,231,000 for right of way.
Scarcely any of the right of way is paid for.
Well, that is the information we want, that is what we want put on the table of the House.
You have the figures here.

Yes, but when the minister comes down with a general statement, showing that the road is supposed to cost $130,000 per mile, surely we must know what the basis of the calculation is. Now, finally, I wish to say that if the present government is not satisfied with the railway as constructed to-day at a cost of $56,000 per mile, the whole thing is in their own hands for the future. From this day on, the Minister of Railways and his commission have to check every dollar of the expenditure; no contractor can get one dollar for any earth he may turn or stone he may blast out, until those now in charge of construction, sign the figures. They can decide what the grades and the curvatures will be, and what the weights of the rails and what kind of bridges will be constructed, and if the balance of the road costs mere than $56,000 per mile, it is they, and they alone, who will be responsible for it. It is the duty of the minister to explain these anomalies which I have pointed out, and I submit that the history of this transaction will be that the men who have had charge of this matter for the late government were men who did the work honestly, with capacity, and with integrity, and their work will stand. We will be ready to compare the result of their efforts with those of the gentlemen who have succeeded them as appointees of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite, and especially my genial and plausible friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), are disposed to treat this matter with a very light touch, but I can assure them that the people of Canada are not disposed to take that view of it. On the Mr. MACDONALD.
late government, and on hon. gentlemen must be the full responsibility for this miscalculation.

What miscalculation?
Mr.	WHITE	(Leeds).	The	miscalculation in the estimated cost of the building of this railway-the miscalculation between $13,000,000 of interest computed by the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the $60,000,000 of interest as shown by the estimate of the Minister of Railways, and the miscalculation	between	the	$54,000,000estimated as the actual cost of construc-toin by the former Minister of Finance, and the appalling figure of $236,000,000, which is found to be the probable actual cost.	The responsibility	for these miscalculations must be assumed by the late government before the people of Canada. There is no use blinking the facts; we must look them straight in the face.

Where is the estimate of $250,000,000?
Mr.	WHITE	(Leeds).	The	amount I
referred to was the $236,000,000 brought down by the Minister of Railways as the total cost of this railway, before the Grand Trunk Pacific Company enters upon the lease, and I think I will be able to satisfy my hon. friend that that estimate is correct. I have no desire to discuss this from a political point of view, but, as I have said before, there is no use blinking the facts. It is my opinion that we will discuss no question in this parliament, having regard either to the large amount of money involved or to the future consequences, which will compare in importance with the question of these figures which we have been discussing in connection with the National Transcontinental railway. I make no charges against the Transcontinental Commissioners, but I do say that there have been rumours of misapplication of moneys, and I do say that the people believe that a great deal of money has been misapplied.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In connection with the construction of the National Transcontinental railway.
Who made the charges ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been charged by some of the engineers, and I say that the people of this country suspect that there has been misapplication of money.
Who suspects that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend keep in touch with public opinion. I make no charge against the commissioners, but I do say that the increase from $13,000,000 interest, as estimated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to the $60,000,000 estimated by the Minister of Railways, and the difference between the $54,000,000 estimated by Mr. Fielding as the total cost of construction, and the $236,000,000 now shown to be the probable cost, these vast differences form ground for a prima facie case against the late government and against the Transcontinental Railway Commission, which they must explain away. Let us review the situation with deliberation. This agreement was entered into in 1903, and 1904, so that the National Transcontinental railway has been under construction for a period of eight or nine years. Now, I propose to consider for a moment the question of miscalculation in estimates.
-Who made it? Mr. Schrieber.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not interrupt.
You start on the wrong premises.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Wait till I get through. The right hon. leader of the opposition, then the leader of the government, is reported in ' Hansard ' as follows:
When completed, the company will lease the road and will pay to us a rental at the rate of three per cent per annum upon the cost of construction, whatever that may be. The same abatement of rent is provided also as in the case of the western section. During seven years the company will be exempt from the payment of rent. For three years the company will be bound to pay the revenues and tolls of the road if they amount to three per cent; and if they fail to amount to three per cent, then the difference between the revenues gathered and the three per cent will be capitalized and added to the cost of construction, and the company will pay interest upon it. So that here again the whole of the liability which is incurred by the government for the building of that section from Moncton to Winnipeg is simply seven years of interest. The sum total of the money to be paid by the government for the construction of that line of railway from Moncton to the Pacific ocean will be in the neighbourhood of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000. and not a cent more. Now, Sir, what is $13,000,000 in the year 1903? It is about the surplus of our revenue over the expenditure. The surplus for this year will pay for the construction of this road.
' Now, I do not for a moment say, although these words might reasonably give that impression, especially to the public, that the entire cost of this road was estimated by the leader of the late government at $13,000,000. What he had in mind, I believe, was this, that the interest charge during the 7 years of operation by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, during which they were to pay no rental, together with some interest charges which he had in mind, would amount possibly to $13,000,000. What are the facts? The fact according to the estimates of the hon. gentleman from (St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), based on the figures given by the hon. Minister of Railways is that the cost to this country will be $60,000,000, or five times the cost estimated by the late government. Is that a matter to be treated lightly, as hon. gentlemen opposite have treated it-an estimate falling short of the actual interest $47,000,000? I say there has not been as great a blunder made in estimating in this country since Confederation as that made of the cost of this National Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Moncton. Take the actual cost. It was shown by thg hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) that my predecessor estimated the cost from Winnipeg to Moncton at $54,000,000. It will not do to say that the government engineer estimated it at $51,000,000 or $52,000,000. In approaching an estimate of this kind it is not wise to go it blind. The government should have informed themselves more fully as to the character of the country through which this road would pass, both from the standpoint of the cost of construction and the standpoint of the traffic which the road would derive when, completed. But apparently no investigation of any kind was made; at all events, if it was, it must have been of the most superficial kind, having regard to the result. Now, what is the result? My predecessor estimated $54,000,000, as the cost, or $28,000 a mile from Winnipeg to Quebec and $25,000, per mile from Quebec to Monct-on. That is specific; there are his figures. It was upon that understanding that the government entered upon the construction of this line. That is the estimate for which the late government must take full responsibility; and what is the outcome? The outcome is that instead of a cost of $54,000,000 from Winnipeg to Moncton, and instead of $28,000 and $25,000 per mile respectively, we have a total cost of $236,000,000, including interest, equal to two-thirds of the net national debt of Canada, and no less than $130,000 per mile. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say, well, we must build the line, and apparently from their arguments this afternoon, it was not of the slightest consequence what the cost would be, because the Grand Trunk Pacific Company must enter on the lease, but it is of the greatest possible consequence, because in the first place no railway can afford to pay a rental beyond a certain amount, I do not care how strong it is; and the first question that arises in this

case is, can the company afford to pay three per cent on the coat of that line, amounting to over $200,000,000, after the first seven years of operation? Now, wha* does that amount to? It amounts to no less than $6,000,000 a year-no less than $20,000 a day of rental to meet the $6,000,000 of fixed charges; and that is over and above the operating expenses. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when in the government, had the idea that this road would reduce freight rates. What is there by way of traffic on that line? It runs through hundreds of miles of desolate wilderness, which will afford no local traffic. What about return freights? The grades are all right, they say; they will bring down trains laden with grain from the west. But what goes back? What hope is there of reducing freight rates in this country, with a fixed charge of $6,000,000 between Winnipeg and Moncton? These are considerations which have been overlooked by hon. gentlemen opposite. Their argument this afternoon proceeded coolly on the assumption that it did not make any difference if the road cost $500,000,000 or a $1,000,000,000, because the Grand Trunk Pacific Company would pay three per- cent of the cost. But I want to tell them that every dollar of the $113,-
853,000	that has been paid out and of the balance of $57,873,000 still to be paid, represents cash to be paid by the people of the Dominion of Canada. There is no blinking that fact. When the leader of the late government estimated $13,000,000 of interest as the entire cost of this line to the people of Canada, what had he in mind? He had this in mind, and no doubt it was logical, that the road when constructed would be operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company on a payment of three per cent on the cost, and that this would carry all the interest on the money which the government would borrow for the purpose of constructing the road, and he estimated that the only thing the country would have to bear would be the $13,000,000. But he had not the slightest conception at the time of the colossal cost of this road as it was ulti-matelv worked out.
Now let us take the western situation, and there you will find miscalculation all along the line, although I believe absolutely in the west and I think I have more confidence in it than some of its representatives here, but I will dwell on that a little later. Take the prairie section of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and it will cost $40,000 a mile. Take the mountain section of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and it will probably cost $70,000 a mile. Now take it from the standpoint of freight rates. If there was anything which justified the late government in going into the construction of a line such as the National Transcontinental railway it was for the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
purpose of regulating the freight rates of the country, of having a line which would regulate them, because there is a clause in the agreement under which the rates are to be arranged subject to revision by the government. Now under the circumstances mentioned what chance is there for a reduction of freight rates? Is there a man on either side of this House who will state that the freight rates can be reduced by reason of the construction of a National Transcontinental on the figures that have been produced here by my friend the Minister of Eailways? I doubt very much if there is any man who has the temerity to suggest any such thing. Even supposing, there is a clay belt to be settled north of the line and industries to be developed, what practical use so far as local traffic is conicexned can Ibe made of the line for years to come from Moncton to Winnipeg? These are some considerations worthy of attention. Supposing the line were completed from Moncton to Winnipeg, what would it be worth without the lease? A line isolated, hung in the air so to speak, without connections? The Grand Trunk Pacific at the time they entered into the agreement for the construction of that line on the estimate of the government contemplated the payment of 3 per cent of the cost of construction which the late Finance Minister estimated at $54,000,000 a year but which has now been shown to amount to no less a sum than $200,000,000, or as I have said $6,000,000 in interest a year. Now when we come to the question of the physical condition of the line all this argument is absolutely relevant to the matter of the commission. I say that the commission had the construction of this line under their charge and under their direction anl I say that if that construction has not gone forward intelligently, if that construction has not been carried on as it 'Should have been carried on according to the best opinion in this country, then I think the responsibility must rest upon the late government. The hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) called attention to the fact that there were certain anomalies in the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. If you look at the statement of items ' National Transcontinental Railway, Eastern Division Road ' you will find the ' Grading, contract items, including peering, excavation, culverts, substructures of bridges, track laying, ballasting, etc., value of work done to December 31, 1911, $79,368,700, and value of work required to complete $13,510,300.' If you look down further you will find: ' Buildings, including stations, section and tool houses, and divisional point buildings, value of work required to complete $3,971,780.' That is where the heavy cost is coming in, not in connection with the grading and track

laying that has been completed according to the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) to the percentage mentioned. Then a little further down you will find a large item $9,051,500. What is that for? ' Terminals at Quebec and line from Quebec bridge to Quebec city. Value of work required to complete $9,051,500.J If you will look at the two columns you will see that a large expenditure has not yet been made upon a number of the items set forth there. You will notice that there is a very heavy expenditure still to be made, so that there is nothing anomalous in my hon. friend's statement. Referring again to the physical condition of that railway, I say that here the late government in my opinion, and the late commission also are responsible, notwithstanding what my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) has said about that. What is the condition of the line from Mountain to Levis? It is very nearly completed we are told, but of what use is it in that unfinished state? Interest is running upon the cost of it. How long will it be before the line is completed so as to be able to take out grain from the west? My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) smiles at that. He is very much interested' in the western situation as we all are. Why is it that grain is not coming down from the west to Cochrane now, and then over the Grand Trank railway to Toronto, why is it the line is not completed to Cochrane, when the line from Levis to Moncton is practically completed? Hon. gentlemen opposite have ibeen rising in their places and blaming the .government for the present situation in the west. I want to tell them that the late government, and the late commission appear to be more blameable than any one else for the present condition of affairs in Canada. There is only one railway line running out to-day from Port Arthur and that is the Canadian Pacific railway line.
And the road from Port Arthur to Winnipeg is not completed yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That section is not yet completed, but as I say there is only one line running out to-day from Port Arthur. You may have as many lines running down to Fort William as you like. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) mentioned the line running down from Superior to Fort William. I do not care if you had ten lines running down there instead of one. That does not help the western situation to-day a bit because there is only one line out from Port Arthur and that is the Canadian Pacific railway line.
What about the Canadian Northern?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not yet constructed.
Does my hon. friend say there is not a line running from Port Arthur to Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But east of Port Arthur there is only one line. Remember it is eight or nine years since this contract was entered into, nine years to complete the line to Cochrane, and it is not completed yet, and m.y hon. friend says it will not be completed for two years. Now who is to blame for the fact that the western grain cannot be moved to the east? Who is to blame for the lack of cars and for all the congestion that we hear of almost daily from hon. members from the west? When the late government were in power did my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) opposite ever rise in his place and tell the government that the line to Cochrane was not completed, and should be rushed no matter what the expenditure might be, in order that the grain might be moved from the east and double the railway facilities from the west? I never heard of it. And my eloquent friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff)-I am sorry he is not here to-night, because I think I can place the blame where it belongs-did he ever rise at any time and ask whether means were being taken to 'double the railway facilities of the west by constructing the line to Cochrane? Not at all. That cannot be gainsaid or denied. What about the line to Superior? The line to Superior even was a year late. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway has been operating its Prairie section for two years. The first year they were unable to take out grain from the west. Why? Because the line from Winnipeg to Superior was uncompleted.
The hon. gentleman knows very well that he is unfair in making a comparison with the prairie section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not unfair. My hon. friend is not the fairest person in the world himself. My hon. friend says I am comparing the construction of a line between Winnipeg and Superior, with the prairie section. My hon. friend is overlooking this fact, which I have made the basis of my argument:	the late
government had eight years in which to construct this railway and what have we got to-day? Why it is like starting to build a house by constructing the chimney instead of excavating and building the basement. You were a year late in getting ta *Superior, and you are three years late- because it will take a year and a half or two years to complete it, between Superior and Cochrane-in getting to Cochrane. Now I ask when we hear about this grain blockade in the west, and about this congestion of cars in the west, upon whose

shoulders is the blame to rest? Let us be fair in this matter; all we want, is fair play. The government has been in power since October 6, and almost daily since the House began its sittings, remarks have been made about our preventing the grain getting out from the west. I do not intend to allow this matter to remain there, but every time I hear this complaint I shall place the blame where it belongs.
Does my hon. friend seriously pretend that the congestion in the northwest to-day is due to the fact that the road between Superior Junction and Cochrane is not completed? Is he serious in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend does not understand the situation.
Are not the elevators full?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course they are full. I thought I had made this matter plain, but apparently I did not. I say, if you had ten lines going to Fort William in winter after the close of navigation, and only one line out from Fort William east, how great is the capacity of your railway? Just as great as that of one line, and no greater. If you have two lines, you double the capacity. One of the greatest complaints of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I think it is one they will not be slow to urge, is that the government has not finished the line between Winnipeg and Cochrane so that they could get the advantage of it. You have the prairie section in operation for two years and only getting down to Fort William last year. So much for the physical condition, except this: First, we have the line from Moncton to Levis almost completed. But what about the Quebec bridge? Where is it? It is in the river. I do not intend to place the responsibility for the fall of the Quebec bridge; unavoidable accidents sometimes happen. I do not propose to apportion the responsibility for that.
Then why do you mention it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because I want to show the situation.
Does the hon. gentleman pretend to argue the condition of the Quebec bridge as a justification for the reduction of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was answering arguments that are brought forward on the other side. And what I say is strictly relevant. I am not wandering one whit further afield than did the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). I am dealing with the situation of this road. We have heard of the great advantages of the road in the west. The hon. member for Assini-Mr. WHITE (Leedsl.	.
boia (Mr. Turriff) told us how it was taking out the grain, and others have told us how it was relieving the situation. I am merely meeting these arguments, and what .1 say is relevant and pertinent to the issue. I am fairly criticising the commission. I have not charged anything against them, but I am fairly criticising them by pointing out the physical condition of the line, and showing the nature of the construction east of Winnipeg. If the commissioners have constructed the line between wrong points or have gone on first with parts of the line which should not have been constructed first, they are fairly open to criticism. Now, the Quebec bridge-I was taking that up when I was interrupted by the hon. member for Halifax-from Moncton to Levis the road is almost completed. But, of what use is it to the country? And as to the Quebec bridge, I was only narrating when interrupted by my hon. friend
I am glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was merely setting forth the historical fact that the Quebec bridge is now in the St. Lawrence. How many years will it be before the Quebec bridge will be capable of forming the last link in the chain between Winnipeg and Moncton? The people have a rough way of adjudicating upon these matters. They judge largely upon results; and if this line has not been completed^ either through the fault of the Quebec bridge^ or for any other reason, they are apt to visit the blame upon the government during whose term this all occurred. I am not going into the question of what responsibility attaches through the falling of the bridge. I am merely stating the situation -and there is the situation. Then, we have the remainder of the road finished or nearly completed, as shown by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane). He estimates that the road should be finished by the 1st of January, 1914
The Quebec bridge in 1917.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, 1917 for the Quebec bridge, and 1914, or two years hence, for the railway. Eight years since the beginning, plus two years more to the finish, makes ten years-ten years for the construction of this line before it is in a position to haul out grain from the west.
The conisiderations that I have mentioned, I think, are of the greatest possible importance, and I think that they are absolutely relevant to this discussion. Now, what is our position as a government ? Our position is that we have fallen heir to this National Transcontinental as a heritage. A damnosa hereditas, or, I would ratheT call it a hereditas damnosa; I think that is 'a little better Latin-but either will

do; and iat all events that is our heritage. On this side of the House we are patriots and Canadians before we axe pa-tisane; and there is not a man on this side who does not want to prosecute this enterprise with the greatest vigour and carry it through to completion. The cry was raised during the elections before the last, ' Let Laurier finish his work.' We will have to finish this work, and we will finish it well. I hope that the end of the National Trans* continental will be better than its beginning; -and I know that the Minister of Railways will carry this enterprise to completion -more economically than the work hitherto has been carried on.
The -minister himself do-es not seem -to think so judging by his estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean, Halifax) consider what the completion of a railway means. You may have a railway with a part of its right-of-way not paid for, and yet complete in a physical sense. You have telegraph lines, stations, round-houses and other such things to provide. The heavy expense comes in connection with these matters; and must be considered when looking at the road from a physical standpoint.
Does the bon. gentleman (Mr. White, Leeds) agree that it is good jjolicy to continue the construction o-f the road with 4-10 per cent grade? Let us -have an answer to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have inherited a situation. When gentlemen have gone ahead and spent $113,000,000 on construction, and have completed the line at different points, it would not be possible to change the grades even if we wanted to. But more than that: My hon. friend is a good lawyer, yet he has overlooked one thing, and that is that there is an agreement between this country and the Grand Trunk railway as to the standard of construction. The question arises, how far can we change that situation? But all that does not alter the fact that these hon. gentlemen opposite estimated this road at only one-fifth of what it has actually cost. That is the great outstanding fact and you cannot forget it nor gloss it over. But it is what they are trying to do-gloss it over. Thirteen millions as against sixty millions; fifty-four millions as against two hundred and thirty-six millions,-how are you going to get away from the logic of these facts?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. White, Leeds) agrees that it is a good policy to build with grades of 4-10 per cent, and will continue that policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is not a man on this side, from the right hon. leader of
the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) down, on his side-and they are down so far as we are concerned-nor on this side of the House either, who would have voted for the National Transcontinental railway if he had known that these figures would be brought down eight years after that agreement was made. I say, where is there a man on either side of this House who would have voted for the National Transcontinental railway if they had known that these figures would be brought down here eight years afterwards? That is why I say that there is nothing we are going to deal with in this parliament that has anything like the importance of this question.
The country does not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The country does think so, and the country is shocked at these figures. Why, Sir, even our hon. friends apposite do not realize what these figures mean-$6,000,000 interest on the line from Winnipeg to Moncton in one year. Now what is our duty? There is not a man on this side of the House that does not want to see the Grand Trunk Pacific railway made a success, that does not want to see it completed through to Prince Rupert, that does not want to see it carried to completion from Moncton to Winnipeg. They know that the country can stand the cost. I want to say this, that the most gratifying feature in this whole matter is that the surplus revenues of this country in the past have been such as to liquidate so large a percentage of the capital cost of that railway. I say that is a most gratifying fact; because I am a patriotic Canadian, I am not a partisan, and I acknowledge the great prosperity of this country during the regime of the late government. Therefore I say there is not the slightest fear for the future. I say, without anticipating the Budget, that we will be able to write off almost the entire expenditure on the National Transcontinental railway for this year, I look forward with faith to the future, and I want honestly and in good faith to carry out this enterprise to completion.
Now the increase in our national debt. Our national debt is of comparative insignificance, having regard to our resources, $340,000,000, not a -large national debt. So I say, speaking as the minister responsible for the finances of Canada, that notwithstanding this expenditure, of which a great part has already been liquidated by our surplus revenue, I look forward without the slightest apprehension from the financial standpoint. It is only proper that I should say this, while we are justly criticising the miscalculation made by our predecessors, and when we are

meeting their arguments, or their cdn-i sures, against us in regard to the existing western situation. I think I may rightly traverse their arguments by presenting the other side. At the same time I am free to say that notwithstanding the enormous expense the position of this country its such that we will be able to carry the work through to completion. I have the greatest possible faith in the west. There is no man in this House who is more interested in the west than 1 am, 1 claim to be as well acquainted with it as any eastern man can be. I say that our western friends from Aflberta and Saskatchewan are continually misrepresenting that country in this House. You have the province of Saskatchewan, probably five per c.ent under cultivation, and ninety-five per cent still to be cultivated; you have the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba capable of immense development, and of sustaining populations in comfort many times the population they have at the present time. I look forward without the slightest apprehension to the western situation. The Grand Trunk Pacific, and the other lines will take care of themselves. What we want in the west, and what this government stands for, is to give additional spouts to that country, and as many as we can. The Grand Trunk Pacific is pushing through to Prince Rupert, the Canadian Northern railway is running another line to Vancouver, and this government stands pledged to the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, another spout to the north; and the Minister of Railways will urge the construction forward of a line between Superior and Cochrane as vigorously as he can, no matter what the expense may be, in order that that link may be completed at the earliest possible moment. Now, with these spouts, two more to the west, one north to Hudson bay, and one east to Cochrane down by the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Timis-kaming and Northern Ontario to Toronto, then with Mackenzie and Mann constructing the Canadian Northern railway and Ontario east from Port Arthur duplicating the line of the Canadian Pacific railway east to Port Arthur, we have all these additional spouts.

When does the hon. gentleman expect the spout to Hudson bay to be completed?
Mr, WHITE (Leeds). Just as quickly as we can complete it. Give us the eight, years time that you had from Winnipeg to Cochrane, and the Hudson Bay road will be completed.
When will that road of the Minister of Railways be completed to Labrador?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are all optimists here, it is only the hon. gentlemen in, opposition who are pessimists. When I was in the west I saw this sign in half-a-dozen hotels, ' If you can't boost don't knock '; and I have heard more knocking of the west from the western members in this House since I came here than I ever heard before. Why, it will take a hundred immigration agents to repair all the damage that has been done by the talk of western members since this session began. What is the situation this year? It is an extraordinary situation, as we all know, a wet year, and a late harvest. We know what the climatic conditions were, and the enormous strain placed upon the railways. The situation is _ extraordinary, it is not normal. Is it fair therefore to dwell upon such a situation and take so gloomy a view of it as our hon. friends opposite are doing? I say they do not fairly represent the west. The west is the land of invincible optimism, the people of the west are the most courageous in Canada, and they are confronting the situation bravely indeed. They know the climatic conditions are responsible for the situation, they know the congested situation west from Fort William, and still they believe thoroughly in their country. Notwithstanding what has been said by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) as to how many bushels of grain it costs to buy an agricultural implement on this side of the line as compared with the cost on the other side of the line, notwithstanding all that, what are the facts? There -must be some permanent attraction in that great country that draws the people from the republic to the south to come in and take up their homes in that land. What happened last year? Notwithstanding all these gloomy pictures that have been drawn by the hon. member for Edmonton and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) what happened last year? 130,000 immigrants came in from the United States to make their homes in the Canadian west, to settle upon the soil of the great west. They get the - advantage of cheaper land, and of better land, and they have continued to come, and will continue to come notwithstanding the pessimistic talk we hear from hon. gentlemen opposite who misrepresent the west. The western representatives will be looked upon as Jeremiahs if they keep on much longer. But the western people do not want Jeremiahs to represent them, they are optimistic, they are men of the greatest possible courage. Next year they will get a good crop, their harvest will come in earlier, and I hope that the conditions of last year will not be repeated for many a long year to come. The railways will be able to take care of the situation better, and hope will again smile

on that great land. I mention these facts to show that our railway systems in the west will be profitable enterprises. There will yet be mixed farming in the west, there will yet be great manufacturers, so I have no fear at all with regard to the railway situation in the west. Those are my views with regard to the west, and with regard to these items of expenditure which the Minister of Railways has brought down to the House.
The late government cannot escape responsibility for this situation, they cannot gloss it over. It cannot be minimized, it was a miscalculation, one of the grossest miscalculations that has ever occurred in this country since Confederation. What the consequences will be, whether, as the hon. member for St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) has said, this government may yet have to assume a part of this responsibility, I shall not venture to prophesy. But you cannot escape two facts, that $13,000,000 estimated by the late Prime Minister as interest, and I must do him the justice to say that he never estimated it as anything else, has grown to $60,000,000 and the $54,000,000 estimated by my predecessor, I have no doubt in all good faith, $28,000 per mile from Winnipeg to Quebec, and $25,000 a mile from Levis to Moncton has now grown into $236,000,000, nearly five times as much and equal to $130,000 per mile. I say that whatever the significance of these figures may be, whatever may be the consequence of that calculation, the responsibility must rest not on the government that finished it, but on the' government that started it, that conceived the project and carried it through almost to completion before we came into power.

Mr. Chairman, rarely have I listened to such a pessimistic speech from a gentleman who claims to be an optimist^ as we have heard this evening. My hon. friend has devoted pretty nearly one half of his very earnest apneal to the people of this country to an effort to convince them that this road will cost $130,000 a mile, and that the late government should be censured for that condition of affairs. My hon. friend knows that is not the case at all.
Order !
He knows that the road will only cost $90,000 a mile.
Order !

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know what cost of construction includes under this agreement ?
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does it include interest?
Under the agreement seven years' interest will be added to the cost of construction for the purpose of paying interest, but these commissioners are not responsible for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say they were.

That is the inference from the statement of the hon. gentleman, that is the statement of the hon. member for St. Antoine, of the hon. member for East Toronto, to-night. These commissioners have nothing to do with the interest, they are simply the medium through which this road is being constructed.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance on one point. He is the first hon. gentleman on the Conservative side of the House who has been fair enough to admit that when the late Finance Minister made the statement about the $13,000,000 he was talking about the interest the country would have to pay and not the cost-of the road.

I would remind my hon. friend that on two occasions at least I distinctly called attention to the fact that I understood the Prime Minister to be re-



ferring to what it would actually cost the country in outlay which it would not get back.	.

I shall have to accept the statement of my hon. friend but 1 could not have been in the House at the time he made the statements. It has been reported from end to end of Canada that this road would cost $13,000,000 only.
Did my hon. friend hear the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) make exactly the same statement as is made by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) this evening?

I was talking about members on the Conservative side of the House, my friends from Peel and froni bim-coe and the others have stated in the House and it has been taken up by every Conservative almost in Canada, that Mr Fielding said this road would cost only $lo,000,000.

I rise to a point of order. V.hen the hon. member says that the member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) on any occasion either in the House or out of it alleged that the late Prime Minister said that this road would only cost $13 000,000 be is making inadvertently a mistatement. I never said so inside or outside the House.

I had accepted my hon. friend's statement, he need not get nervous. I am glad the Minister of Finance has forced these gentlemen to come out in the open and make the statement that they did not mean that we said that this road would cost $13,000,000. What Mr. Fielding said was that as he figured it the interest charges would be $13,000,000. Mr. Fielding was in error, there is no question about that.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends say ' hear, hear I would like to know if Mr. Fielding was the first public man who was ever guilty of an error of judgment in discussing a great public work. Any hon. gentleman who has ever built himself a house knows that the cost exceeded the estimate of his architect. Have they ever heard of a public work that did not cost more than they figured? But my hon. friends say it costs too much more. Let us take the conditions at the time the statement was made. It was made in 1903. No surveys had been made, no expert information had been obtained. The government took the statement of Mr. Schreiber, then deputy Minister of Railways and Canals. Mr. Schreiber told them that in his opinion the road could be built for about $30000 a mile. It happens that Mr. Schreiber was wrong. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) complains of the delay

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That does not include interest.
No, that is for the construction of the road proper. I admit we have to pay interest.
And under the contract they are to add the interest for seven years.
I appreciate that.
And that adds to the cost of the road.
Yes, so far as interest is concerned, and, therefore, the road if it be a success must pay interest on the interest as well as on -the actual cost.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I understand it, not
only by custom, but also by the terms of the contract, interest must be calculated.

I am not begging the question at all; I am admitting that according to the contract you must add the interest to the cost of construction for the purposes of the interest earning capacity of the road. The Minister of Finance tells us that there will be about $3,500 per mile of interest annually and he does not believe that the road can pay that interest. Well, I am not a railway manager and, therefore, I cannot -give an absolute answer to that from experience, but I think I can give a pretty good answer from the experience of other roads. I find on looking over the annual report of the Canadian Pacific railway for 1909 that there was of capital stock, preference stock, consolidated debenture stock, and mortgage bonds, outstanding at that time, $372,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How many miles of road?

About 9,000 miles of road at that time. I think I am safe in saying that on that the Canadian Pacific railway pays in dividends -and interest from six to seven per cent annually. They are paying a higher rate of interest now but for the purposes of calculation I will take the figures as they were then. Thus it will be found that the Canadian Pacific railway in the 9,000 miles, including branch lines, cheaply constructed lines of every kind, roads that do not pay, hundreds of miles of railway that never paid; all included they are paying about $2,500 per mile interest, and we know they have a surplus sufficient to pay if they wish to, another $2,500 per mile interest.
Does that include their land sales?

It -does not. I, therefore, say that the earnings of the Canadian Pacific railway to-day are sufficient to pay $5,000 per mile interest. But says the Minister of Finance, the Grand Trunk Pacific is going through a district that is not settled, and that I admit, but I leave it to the Minister of Railways who knows the country traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific, if it d-s not a f-ar better country than two-thirds of the country travelled by the Canadian Pacific railway from Winnipeg to Montreal. There are a few more people on the Canadian Pacific railway from Winnipeg to Montreal than there will be at first on the Grand Trunk Pacific line, but I am told by engineers who have been in that country that it includes a territory five hundred miles long by two hundred miles wide and that it contains a gread deal of the finest arable land on the continent, so that the country traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific will assuredly be the home of thousands, yes, of millions of people, in the. near future. This railway traverses a wooded country from 150 miles east of Winnipeg to Quebec and on down through New Brunswick, and does any man tell me that a road traversing a country like that will not earn as much as the Canadian Pacific railway does between Winnipeg and Montreal?
Do not the figures which my hon. friend has given include the hotel system, and the steamship lines?

I do not think they include the steamship lines. They may include the hotels, but they are a mere bagatelle, and I presume they are run at a loss. But even if the figures do include the steamship lines, there is such a margin every year that the line will still pay $4,000 to $5,000 a mile and have a surplus. The Canadian Pacific railway has grown rich through transcontinental business. Take away the transcontinental business

which that company gets at Winnipeg and I do not suppose they -would feel like maintaining the tracks from Winnipeg to Montreal; and what is true of the Canadian Pacific railway will be true of the National Transcontinental railway. It will cover just as much territory west of Winnipeg; it will get just as much freight to haul; it will have just as much business to do; it will have just as much return traffic; it ought to be in a few years just as big an institution from a business standpoint; and if the Canadian Pacific railway can pay $4,000 or $5,000 a mile of interest, I do not see how any man can say that the National Transcontinental cannot pay $3,500 a mile. But there is something else that my hon. friends fail entirely to recognize in discussing this question. It has been stated by some hon. gentlemen, and strongly intimated by the hon. member for St- Antoine (Mr. Ames), that this road has cost too much. I deny that, and I say that it would be a misfortune for Canada if this road had cost one dollar less than it has cost, provided that cost has been honestly expended.	,
Does the hon. gentleman refer to the last $10,000,000?

Yes, I will include that as well, although I was not referring to it at the time. I will say that the last $10,000,000 was well expended. When that road is completed, it will be the best asset the Dominion of Canada has ever had or will have in the lifetime of any living man. Perhaps there are not many gentlemen here who have taken the trouble to investigate the earning possibilities of a road with a grade of only four-tenths of one per cent, as compared with the ordinary grade of from 1 to 14 per cent, which is to be found on all the other roads in Canada.
I have taken the trouble to investigate certain sections of road. The Canadian Pacific railway, from Montreal to St. John, which is indicative of the ordinary roads through Canada, can transport, with the best engine it owns to-day, about 600 tons of freight per train. Take the same engine and put it on the International railway from Montreal to St. John, and it will handle hardly 1,200 tons. The same engine, put on the Grand Trunk Pacific from Quebec to St. John, with the assistance over two short pusher grades, will transport over 2,000 tons under exactly the same conditions. But take the same engine from the Rocky Mountains to Quebec, without a pusher grade of any kind, and it will transport over 2,000 tons. That is done with the same coal consumption, the same trackage cost, the same overhead expenses. You have three times the earning capacity in the one case that you have in the other. When you have millions of tons of freight trom the great west-because that is where | Mr. CARYELL.
the freight comes from for the Canadian Pacific railway and for the Canadian Northern, and will come from for the Grand Trunk Pacific-does any man tell me that when the Canadian Pacific railway can pay interest of from $4,000 to $5,000 a mile, this road will not be able to pay $3,500 a mile? One Iras only to state the proposition to demonstrate how unreasonable is the argument of the Finance Minister. Then, you have the undeveloped local traffic which will be developed. You have a thousand miles of primeval forest through which the road will pass; you have a thousand miles of territory which has hardly yet been invaded by man; you have all that lumber to transport and all the supplies to go in, and the men to develop that great industry. I come next to the question, has this road cost more than it should cost? Unless my hon. friends contend that it has, they must admit, if they would be logical, that it will be the greatest carrier ever built on the continent, and I believe in the world, for its length. I wonder if these hon. gentlemen know the kind of road that this road will be when completed. Some of them have seen the prairie sections of the road, but very few have seen that portion from Winnipeg to Moncton. I have not had the privilege of going over the whole, but I have gone over a considerable portion of it-on handcar, on flat car and on engine, therefore I think 1 know something of what I am talking about when I say that I believe there is not such a road in America, and 1 know there is not in Canada. It will he absolutely complete when handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company two or three years hence. The' grading is absolutely perfect. There are probably two or three "times the number of culverts that are to be found on an ordinary road, and all of concrete or stone. Nothing has been saved in the way of drainage, or in the way of road-bed ballast; the station houses are to he complete; every mile will be fenced with the most secure and substantia] fence. Now, the Minister of Railways and Canals made the statement that in his judgment, or in the judgment of some-bod v else nearly $8,000,000 will be required in the next eight or nine years for betterments on this road; and just here the minister will perhaps tell me whether these figures are the estimates of Mr. Grant or not. I would like to know if that statement of betterments came with Mr. Grant's sanction?
I am not sure whether it was by Mr. Grant or Mr. Leonard.

I have'nothing derogatory to say concerning Mr. Leonard, but I want to tell my hon. friend that these figures would appeal to me with very much greater- force if it came from Mr. Grant

rather than, from Mr. Leonard. What I am trying to get into my bon. friend's head in that there never was1 a road built in Canada or the United States like the National Transcontinental. I do not believe that Mr. Grant ever made the statement that the road would require nearly nine million dollars of betterments in the next ten years. Therefore you can cut out that $8,000,000 with one stroke of the pen, and you will be perfectly safe in doing so. Now, I come down to the next branch of the case; that this road cost more than it should cost. That is a very important question, because it is all very well for the Minister of Finance to get up here in a pessimistic manner

An lion. MEMBER. Optimistic.

No, pessimistic, and say the people are not disposed to treat this matter lightly, and that they believe there has been a great misappropriation of money in the classification of the road. Does the Finance Minister know that the original contract provided for a commission to settle this question of classification, and that a committee of three of the ablest engineers in Canada
Blockers. [DOT]
I think the hon. gentleman should withdraw the statement that Mr. Schreiber, Mr. Grant and Mr. Keliiher are three of the ablest blockers- in Canada.
I thought you referred to the commission.
Will my hon. friend withdraw the statement?
Certainly.

I am glad of that, because if the hon. gentleman had been listening he would not have made the statement he did. It is in the same class with the statement he made last Wednesday night, when he said that the curtain lias rung down on the gentlemen responsible for building this road and that they should go into oblivion as soon as possible, and that if hey were allowed their liberty they should be grateful. I have not any brief to defend the gentlemen who formed that commission, but I think that so far as honesty is concerned and their dealings with the people of Canada, their records will bear comparison with many of their tradueers.
Mr. CURRIEi Was there not over classification discovered on the Transcontinental railway?

We have had an investigation of the classification by a committee of this House, also by a board of arbitration, consisting of Messrs. Keliiher,
Grant and Schreiber, and what is the result? That out of some fifty or sixty million dollars on classified work on this road, they cut out in district F, about $300,000 or $400,000, and I think in district B, something like $150,000.
How much on the Winnipeg section?

That is district F, about $300,000. Anyway, it is less than half a million. I want to tell my hon. friends opposite that not 5 per cent, of that was the result of over-classification, but was due to a change in overbreak The arbitration held that the engineers had allowed too much for overbreak, and therefore, it was not a matter of overclassification. In plain English the contractors had taken out too much excavation, they removed more material than was necessary, and were not entitled to be paid for it, and a reduction was made of from $300,000 to $500,000. In district B there was also a slight reduction due to overclassification, and with these three exceptions so far as I know, there has not been one dollar taken off the engineer's estimate for classification and overbreak.
Why have they not paid -the contractor?
What contractor?
The contractor west of Cochrane, there is a dispute in regard to that contract yet.

I want to tell my hon. friend that so far as the arbitrators have gone, that is the net result of their investigation. He and his friends here may rest assured that no investigating commission will ever take off anything appreciable trom the charges, by reason of classification or overbreak. More than that, when this investigation is finished, you will be surprised to find out how nearly the results will agree with the results- returned by the rnginecrs of the late Transcontinental Commission.
I hope so.

Furthermore, I tell the minister that he cannot probe the New Brunswick end of the Transcontinental too carefully to suit me, and every member from that province, and also to satisfy every contractor on that line, to say nothing of the commissioners. I know the excellent condition of things he will find in New Brunswick, and the same good results will be found all over the remainder of the road. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell u? that this railway has cost too much. Do they take into consideration the fact that [DOT]hree fourths of the cost consist of labour which has gone up from thirty-five to fifty per cent, in the last seven or eight years?
Do they also consider that supplies have advanced from 25 to 30 per cent, in that time? Do they also consider the fact teat a line with a four-tenths grade has been constructed?
Does not the hon. gentleman think that labour is dearer than when the road was started?
I know it is; I don't ' think ' it.

But that would hardly account for it, would it?-in view of the fact that these contracts were let at schedule rates before the rise in the price Vif labour took place? These contracts were made as far back as 1905, I presume. In that case the rise in the price of labour would hardly account for what the hon. gentleman has mentioned.

To some extent it would, because there was labour that was not anticipated at that time. It would be interesting if we were able to make a comparison between the cost of this road and other great roads on the continent. But I am afraid that only the railway companies themselves could give us the exact figures. But we can get somewhere near the matter, and I propose to give my hon. friend some of the information that 1 have Deen able to extract from the authorities whom I have consulted. I have here statistics on railways in the United States and Canada furnished by the Interstate Commerce Commission down to 1908. Let us consider the case of the Canadian Pacific railway. The commission gives the amount of outstanding stocks and bonds and other securities in 1908 as $327,675,000.^ Uns makes an average of $58,000 per mile. So far as the bonds and debenture stock and the preference stock are concerned, I am satisfied that they sold at par. So far as the stock of the Canadian Pacific railway is concerned, it is almost impossible to tel] what it realised for the road. We know that the first $25,000,000 was sold as low as 25 per cent, 35 per cent, or 50 per cent. But we know also that later issues have sold at par, and the latest was sold, I believe, at 160. Average it up and you will find that the stock of the Canadian Pacific railway has produced pretty near par, and, of course, the bonds have produced par. Now, admit that the stock and bonds of the Canadian Pacific railway produced par, and you have an average cost for the 9,154 miles of this system at that time-including branch lines, colonization roads and all the rest, of over $58,181 per mile.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does that include rolling stock?

I cannot tell; it is not siiown here. We know that probably some Mr. CARVELL.
part of that issue was spent for rolling stock, and we know certainly that millions >f earnings have gone into rolling stock and into betterments. I have acknowledged 'hat it is hard to get accurate figures; I give the committee the best I have got. if they are not logical and reasonable, then they are worth nothing. If we admit that $58,000 a mile would be a reasonable amount for the main line on the basis of these figures, then consider something further. We gave the Canadian Pacific railway when it was incorporated about 835,000,000 or $40,000,000 of completed works; that is a matter of history. We also gave them $25,000,000 in cash. And a few years afterwards we loaned them for he purpose of completing their road, $30,000,000 in cash. We know that these three items went into the main line. You have a total there of $95,000,000 to be divided iver 3,000 miles in length of the main line, or about $32,000 a mile extra. Add that o the $58,000 already given, and you have 890,000 for the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway-as compared with $95,000 for the main line of the Grand Trunk ''acifie.
Was not 'he $30,000,000 returned?
Of course it was.
Was it not paid out of the capital stock of the company?

No.
Mr. WILSON	(Wentworth). Are you
sure?

No. I have admitted that these figures are only the best I can and. There have been stock transactions and earnings that have gone into the road, and it is pretty hard to form an accurate estimate.
