But if 1 am anywhere near correct, you have $90,000 a mile as the cost of the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway. But no man would tell is for a moment that the mam line of the Canadian Pacific railway is anywhere up to thei standard of the mam line of the Transcontinental. We know that it lias not cost so much money, and it ought not to have cost so much money; it has not the transportation facilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific; it is not in it for a moment with the Grand Trunk Pacific Now, these inures bring us down to 1908. My non. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) could 'ell better than I can something of what the Canadian Pacific lias spent in bettering their lines since 1908. I can speak about the branch line on which I live, which rUns from Macadam Junction to iertn. They spent on that since 1908 over $1,000,000 or $10,000 a mile. And this on a branch line. We know that they have

spent two or three millions in the west tunneling through the mountains. We know that they have spent immense sums in the -great Viaduct at Lethbridge. We know that they have practically rebuilt the main line since 1908. Mr. WILSON. (Wentworth). But all this is included in what the hon. gentleman has already doubled up three or four times. Mr. CARVELL. The hon. gentleman has not listened to me. I have told him that these figures are down to 1908; and now 1 am giving him facts to indicate that tens of millions have been spent since then. Yet the road has never got up to the standard of the Transcontinental and never will, it is impossible. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not like to listen to these figures. And no wonder. They say that the road has cost too much, while we contend that it has not. And we put forward the facts that we have the greatest road on the continent, a road that has been honestly built, every dollar of which has been honestly expended. We court the fullest investigation. And when you have an investigation, as I hope you will, the commissioners will report to the government and the government to the country that we have the finest road on the continent,^ a road that will pay interest from the day it is handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific. And it will not be more than three or four years before hon. gentlemen opposite will be taking credit to themselves for this great proposition which will bring such benefit both to the east and to the west. The Minister of Finance (Mr. White) says that if the road had been completed, we should not have had the grain blockade of to-day. I am not prepared to assent to that statement, but, on_ the other hand, I will not quarrel with him. If we had the road completed we could handle grain that is not now handled. If the Canadian Northern railway were completed, the same would be true. But all this bears out the wisdom, the statemanship of the right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) of the government under which this work was inaugurated. It all bears testimony to the leadership and ability of the men who are building the road and the good judgment they have exercised not only in starting the building of the road when they did but in starting to build that kind of line that is being constructed. Nothing will go down in history which will redound more to the credit of Canadian stasesmen than this great Transcontinental will to the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was leader of the House at that time. I want my friends opposite and their friends throughout the country to address themselves, ii they can, to this aspect of the case. If they nan prove that this road has cost more	than it should have cost, I shall be perfectly willing to admit the corn and say that we are wrong. But until we have evidence of that I stick to what I have said -that this road has not cost a dollar more than it should have cost or a dollar more than the people will get results for. There is another thing which these hon. gentlemen seem to forget. And that is that this money has not been given away, as the money was given away by the friends of the hon. gentlemen opposite for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. I am not going to find fault with the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. I want to bear testimony to the fact that it was one of the great works of one of the great men of Canada. Without the Canadian Pacific railway the great west would not have been opened up. But when you compare what the Canadian Pacific railway has cost this country with what the Grand Trunk Pacific has cost, the latter pales into insignificance. We gave the Canadian Pacific railway $25,000,000 in money, $40,000,000 in constructed work, and 25,000,000 acres of land. Those 25,000,000 acres of land have been partly sold, I think they have about. 10,000,000 acres left. Mr. COCHRANE. What were they worth when we gave them? Mr. CARVELL. What are they worth now? Suppose they gave away the 15,000,000 acres that are gone, and they have only the 10,000,000 acres left, why, these 10,000,000 are worth $300,000,000 to-day. They have got probably $200,000,000 out of what they have sold, or $100,000,000 any way; so we have given them altogether $400,000,000 worth of land. They have given all that away to the Canadian Pacific railway in addition to the $05,000,000 or $70,000,000 given in actual cash or in constructed works. What have we done? The very worst case which even the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) can make out is that we are losing $60,000,000 in interest. But remember that we are getting a' splendid piece of property, a property which is ours, it is not the property of the Grand Trunk. We are building a road for ourselves, wc own every rail and every sleeper in it. We are leasing it to the Grand Trunk for forty- * three years, for which they pay interest on it, and at the end of fifty years they hand us back our property in the same condition in which they received it. Does any one mean to tell me that at the end of fifty years this road will not be worth the $200,000,000 we are putting into it? I would be ashamed to call myself a Canadian if I did not have sufficient faith in this country to believe that in fifty years that road will be worth $500,000,000. I consider it was the most magnificent trade the late government ever made. The greatest bargain they ever

made for the country, for the present and for posterity, was when they were able to induce this company to go into the construction of this road. It will not cost the country more than $60,000,000 interest at the end of fifty years, and the $60,000,000 interest will be paid back three or four times over by the appreciation in the value of the property. Now if I am right in my arguments and if I am right in my conclusion, then I say the Minister of Railways is not justified in dismissing from office those three commissioners who have so honestly and so earnestly attempted to carry out their important work in the interest of this country. Is it not a piece of political spite, which is almost'too small to be expected from men who have just-come into office? Would it not have been better to wait a little while and investigate? But no, it seems that the place hunters were so powerful that something had to be done and it was necessary to dismiss these commissioners from office.
Where does the Bill speak about place hunters?

It is like the rest of the commission. They take a man who has occupied a subordinate position for six or seven years, and for some reason was unable to get promotion, and they have promoted him and given him $2,500 a year more than he got before. I want to tell my hon. friend he will be the first man to regret the course this government is taking in removing from office the men who know the conditions, and who have had oversight of this work down -to the present time. I want to tell him something else that he doesn't know; he does not realize the fight these commissioners have had with the Grand Trunk and with the contractors.
I never heard anything of that. We only heard of this commission fighting for the contractors, and against the country -all through.

My hon. friend has not been so far behind the scenes as I thought he had -been. Let me tell him this, the commissioners did fight for the country and against the contractors, and there is hardly a contractor on the line that does not feel he has been improperly treated, because the commissioners have held them down, and have not allowed them to make the profits they hoped to make. The hon. gentleman will know this before very long. For these reasons, I feel that this is ill advised legislation, and the minister would do well to reconsider the rash step he has taken, and not proceed with this Bill.

I have listened, as a new member, with a great deal of interest to this debate, and to what has been said by those responsible for what I think is one
' Mr. CARVELL.
of the most gigantic public crimes that has ever been perpetrated in the history of Canada. It is amusing almost to listen to the remarks that are made to justify the action of the late government with regard to the Transcontinental railway. As I listened to the last speaker (Mr. Car veil), I was impressed with the remarkable knowledge of detail and insight he seemed to have of this question from the contractors' standpoint, for a man who is not in any sense interested in the -work.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to insinuate that I am interested?

I was saying that I was very much surprised to note the intimate knowledge the hon. member had in discussing this question. I was going to say, when he interrupted me, that I must compliment him upon the means he has taken to secure that knowledge, riding up and down the line on a hand car, a locomotive, or a flat car, studying the situation. Possibly if we nad had the privilege of studying the question as intimately as he has clone, we might be able to speak with more authority on the details of the construction. But I would like to remind hon. gentlemen opposite of this statement of the Minister of Finance, that here is a road which we were told a few years ago, was to cost a certain figure and we find out that it has cost aproximately five times that figure. I also want to call attention to the contradictory arguments that have been presented by lion, members opposite on that question, compared with their statements made a few days ago, with regard to the condition of crops and grain in the Northwest. One set of hon. members tell us they don't care about a railway that connects the prairie provinces with the eastern and western waterways, they only care about an outlet to the south. On the other hand, it was the proud policy of the leader of the late government, in bringing forward his Bill for the construction of this railway, that it was to join the cast with the west of this continent^ I submit that these arguments are entirely inconsistent. We claim on this side of the House that our policy has been consistent throughout, our policy is to give the prairie provinces relief at the earliest possible moment. As the Minister of Finance has pointed out, that portion of the road from the prairies eastward to Cochrane has been practically neglected.
Further, the western portion, which would have given an all-the-year-around outlet for the grain to Vancouver and Prince Rupert is scarcely started. That was to be completed in 1911, and there is only constructed a few miles from Prince Rupert eastward, and a short distance

through the Yellowhead Pass. There is an outlet which could have been easily completed in 1911, and which would have given a very material relief to the congested conditions of the grain areas of the prairie provinces.
The hon. gentleman has. told us in criticising the action of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that all the facts in connection with this railway have been before this country for 4 or 5 years. If they were aware of these facts why is it they did not once raise their voices to have the road completed at an early date? They complain about adding interest to the cost of the road although there has been a delay of two or three years. Any business man will agree that in any constructive work until that work is completed and revenue producing, you must charge up to capital the interest on the money during construction and the longer you delay the time of construction the greater will be the amount of interest charged up. I protest that that interest must be added to the cost of construction which thus becomes $130,000 per mile. Some comparisons were made. The hon. member stated that the Canadian Pacific railway had issued $350,000,000 worth of stock, debentures and preferred stock.
I stated $170,000,000. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), asked me if steamships were included in this estimate. I find they were to the extent of $18,000,000.

Take a total stock debenture issue of $350,000,000 and it comes to $37,500 a mile. That also includes the rolling stock, a very material factor, and includes betterments down to 1908. Another very unjust statement was made by the hon. member. He included the $30,000,000 which had been repaid, and must necessarily have been repaid out of the capital stock of the company or the proceeds of its sale. So the Canadian Pacific railway cost $37,000 a mile, and the hon. member should keep in mind that when the Canadian Pacific railway was built it went through a practically uninhabited wilderness, it was an engineering feat that was thought to be an impossibility, and one of the great members of the Liberal party said that the Canadian Pacific railway would not pay for axle grease. As a matter of fact the Canadian Pacific railway has been a national and a financial . success, and has not cost anything like the figures suggested by the hon. member, whereas with all the facilities for transportation of supplies which the present line has to within a very short distance of the actual construction, this road is costing $130,000 a mile, and the hon. member does not think it is costing a cent too
much. The question is so simple and plain to the people of this country that it is viewed as one of the most gigantic public crimes in the history of the country.
Speaking of the land grants to the Canadian Pacific railway, if we were discussing the construction of that railway now I would strongly oppose the granting of a large land bonus but it is well-known that when that road was under discussion the land grant was not only a necessity but the land given was practically valueless, and was so until within the last few years, when, -yith the development of the country it has assumed considerable value. The hon. member believes that it has a value of $30 an acre and when he asks us to accept these statements it would be well for him to look at the figures of the Grand Trunk Pacific in their present light and not in the light of other days.
Hon. members should remember that two sections of the road that should have been completed two years ago, are scarcely commenced, and that is one of the reasons and the chief reason why we now have such congestion in the west, and I trust that the present Minister of Railways and the present administration will see to it that the Pacific division of the National Transcontinental railway and the division from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, are pushed to an early conclusion in order to give us this relief, which is so much needed in the west.
The minister might have given more light on the portion of the road remaining to be completed, as compared with the charge which he puts in his estimate.
I think I have given a pretty clear detailed statement.

But he has not explained the reasons for that detailed statement. The details are there but the reasons for them are not. I am not a railway builder or the Minister of Railways, and I must say it seems peculiar to me that a road which has been ironed for over 1,400 miles and which has been graded for nearly 1,600 miles, still is only two-thirds completed so far as cost is concerned. That is rather a peculiar statement and calls for some explanation. It must be that my hon. friend has in some way secured an adjustment of the figures which is not apparent upon the face of the statement.
A road that is within less than twenty-five per cent of completion, should not cost thirty-three and one-third per cent to complete, and yet that is the statement the Minister of Railways puts before us.
There is one item of nearly nine million dollars for the terminals in Quebec.

Precisely, and that is what I want to come to. The Bill before us is a question as to the propriety of decreasing the number of members of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, and our discussion has been on the merits of the policy of the government. It has seemed good' to our friends on the other side of the House to lay blame upon the members of the commission because of what they are pleased to call the shortcomings in the policy of the late government. Now, I want to know from the minister if this large charge which he puts in here as the prospective cost of the Quebec terminals is properly chargeable to the commissioners whom he proposes to discharge.
The head engineer gave a signed statement there, and he was the head engineer under the late commissioners.

I am not questioning the figures. Will the minister listen to me, and follow what I am trying to get him to tell me. I am not questioning that the terminals will cost the amount stated here, but I am asking him if he is charging that the ministers are responsible for that proposed expenditure.

I have not charged the commissioners with one single thing;
I have not even criticised the commissioners.

I do not use the word * charge ' in the sense of the minister alleging anything against the commissioners. What I am asking him is whether he says there is anything wrong in the action of the commissioners, or of the late government with respect to these terminals.
That you will have to settle between yourselves.

I do not think there is anything to settle about it. There is no question whatever that it is a matter chargeable to the government and not to the commissioners. The whole argument of gentlemen onnosite has been that because the railroad has cost so much the commissioners must he to blame.
I am not blaming the commissioners.

Not to push this argument too far, I think it would be more decent for the minister to make allegations against the commissioners he proposes to dismiss rather than to present a Bill to the House providing for their dismissal, and have his followers on the back benches make insinuations which they cannot support, and which the minister does not daTe to. I think that position is absolutely unfair. If these men are being dismissed for fault, let the minister get up and say so, Mr. COCHRANE.
and if they are not being dismissed for fault, I think it is absolutely improper that bis followers should get up and make insinuations against the commissioners. Of course, criticism of the policy of the late government is perfectly legitimate; the late government must stand or fall by its policy and take the consequences, but it is not right that the commissioners should be charged by the supporters of the government with that for which if blame there is, the late government was to blame and not the commissioners. There has been nothing brought before the House to warrant the purpose of this Bill. If the suggestion is that the commissioners have been incompetent, there has been nothing brought before the House to show them incompetent, and if the suggestion is that two men can handle the completion of this railroad better than four, I submit that that yet remains to be shown.
It is a question of policy.

As to the suggestion that these commissioners were being dispensed with to save expense; my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) was very strong on the point that we had now a government of economy and the Minister of Railways was going to economize on the Transcontinental Railway Commission by dismissing three of these commissioners. But, as a matter of fact, we have two men on salaries to-day equal to the salaries paid to two of the late commissioners, so that all the Minister of Railways is saving is the salary of two ot the commissioners and not even of three.
That is not a fair statement, because the other man got $5,000 a year, and he was in the employ of the commissioners before.
I suppose the gentleman in question is not double; he is still discharging the same duties as he was discharging before he received extra pay?
The same duties.
Is he discharging the same duties as he discharged before, or is some one else discharging these duties?
We have not taken on any one else.

I am not able to understand what the position of the Minister of Railways is in this respect, but we need, not quarrel about that. At the present time we have two men doing administration that was done by tour, and the two men are getting the same salaries as two of the four were getting. That is unquestionable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not true in that sense.

Well I have made my statement which appears to be a statement of fact, and we need not delay all night on that question. There are two men to-day administering the business of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, and these two men are drawing the same salaries as the two other men who previously assisted in that administration. I suppose that is right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, but one of these men is also doing the same work for which he was paid $5,000 a year before.

Then, either he was doing very little work before, or he is doing very little extra work now. If he was doing $5,000 worth of work in the position he previously occupied he is not able to discharge these duties and take the position of Assistant Chief Commissioner and earn $7,500 a year in that capacity. If the change has been made it is because it means that somebody else will have to toe hired to do the work that Mr. MacPherson formerly did, if the work is to be done efficiently. Now, Mr. Chairman, what 's the use of talking about administering the expenditure for the completion of this Transcontinental road by one or two men less or more; there is a stupendous work to be done; there is a stupendous amount of supervision to be exercised, and, unless, you have the men to exercise that supervision it is not going to be well done and there is going to be loss and not gain. If the men who have been commissioners have been dishonest or incompetent then certainly they should not remain in their positions, but, presuming them to be honest and competent there is nothing in the argument that they have been dismissed as a measure of economy. It is true that two-thirds of the total expenditure has toeen paid on the Transcontinental road and that one-third only remains to be paid. But is it not also a fact that it is in closing up the expenditure that the greatest necessity exists for experienced supervision? Is it not also true that as the work of construction is being closed up, there will arise the question of the operation of certain sections of this completed and partly-corji-pleted road, and is it not advisable and desirable, in the interest of the country, that there should be commissioners of experience and of reliability to take charge of the arrangements for traffic as well as for construction? Instead of there being less work to do, there is more work to do, of a kind that men of the standing of the commissioners are most capable of doing. It is not now merely a matter of construction; it is a matter of being sure that the work has been properly finished, and of making traffic arrangements that will be
both for the benefit of the country and for the benefit of the road itself.

The hon. member is aware, is be not, that those traffic arrangements are all laid down in the statute and in the contract, and that if the Grand Trunk Pacific company sees fit to take over a portion of the road as it is completed, it can do so; and if it does so, the statute provides that it shall take it over on the same terms as the whole, that is, on the basis of 3 per cent. There is no difficulty about arranging anything, because it is all arranged.

any way of constructing railways without paying for them, they will certainly have found a good lino for the benefit of the country. The late government never made that discovery; they were able only to get what they paid for, and in doing that they considered they were doing their duty by the country and the country was doing well. Now, there was no other way of getting a first-class road from the prairies to the seaboard than by paying for it; and whether the present leader of the opposition was mistaken or not as to what it would cost, makes no difference whatever in the ultimate result. The country needed the construction of that railway; the late government entered upon that project; the railway is now being constructed; and no government could exist in Canada that would not carry that project to completion, according to the standards of construction which have prevailed up to the present time. When any horn, friend came to office, his first act was to call off work on that construction, but lie put it back again very quickly. If he ever had any intention of stopping construction, he got inside information on the subject very soon, and he decided wisely that the work- should go on.
Where did they call off the work?
It \vas announced in the press.
I am not answerable for that.
I am glad to know that my hon. friend did not call off the work, but an announcement to that effect was made in the newspaper press supporting the party with which he is associated.
I am not responsible for that.

At any rate the announcement was made and it was not denied. It was announced that he had called off work on the Hudson Bay railway, but he took another think after that and gave orders for it to be restarted.
If I had known what the port would be, the project would have been pressed much faster, but the hon. gentleman and his friends did not have any port to start with.
We did not, have any port to start with and my hon. friend has not got any port yet although he has ordered the. construction to go on.
You are not sure of that.

Yes I am absolutely sure that the Minister of Railways has not decided	which port the
railway is going to. I am not so sure Mr. OLIVER.
that this work is to be recommenced. But the newspapers have announced the fact, and the minister has not stated that the newspapers were mistaken.
I do not contradict everything in the newspapers any more than I contradict a lot of statements which are made in this House.
I am sure the House would be interested to- have a statement from the minister on the subject.
Let us go on with this Bill.
The minister introduced the question of the Hudson Bay railway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
introduced it himself.

I beg the Prime Alinister's pardon. However, if the minister does not see fit to answer a question in regard to a matter he introduced himself that is his business. I must say he seems to have a great lack of information in regard to the business of his department.
I gave too much, that is the trouble.

In regard to a necessity for the early completion of this railway I do not think there should be any question about it. We are all agreed that the railway must be completed at the earliest possible moment and according to the standard laid down in the contract.
The hon. member for Pictou (Air. Alacdonald) did not say that a few minutes ago. In that respect you differ from him.
Not at all.
Yes the member for Pictou most decidedly said that we could complete it according to any grade we liked.

The hon. gentleman said a few moments ago that we were bound to complete it according to the standard established by his government, and that no government could stand that would do anything else. That is quite a different idea.

Not at all. I say that this government, although its supporters are tlo-day criticising the policy under which the road was constructed, up to the present time do not dare to change that standard of construction, although as the member for Pictou said they have the privilege of doing so if they dare. But they do not dare. The Alinister of Railways had no hesitation in calling off the contract on the Hudson Bay railway, and I suppose he could do the same on the

Transcontinental as well. I have made the statement that all the criticism that has been levelled against the bargain made by the government, and the carrying out of that bargain by hon. gentleman opposite, falls to the ground in the face of the fact that they themselves do not dare now to deviate from that standard, and are compelled by public opinion to build the road according to it, although the expense may run to the figures that they have placed before the House. Therefore there is no accusation against the members of the late Transcontinental Commission, nor against the late government in regard to this policy.
Will the hon. gentleman say that the railway as so far completed is up to the standard of the Grand Trunk Pacific as set forth in the agreement with that company?
Yes.
I do not think so when a large amount of sipruee ties have been used by the Grand Trunk Pacific for hundreds of miles along their line.
I do not know what my hon. friend is talking about, and I do not think he knows himself. I heard a reference to spruce ties. May I ask to what part of the line that applies?
To the Grand Trunk Pacific.

If the hon. gentleman had said that I would have understood him. Now in regard to the standard of this road and in regard to its serviceable character, one would have thought from what has been said that no one had any control over the construction except the Transcontinental Commission or the government. According to the bargain "made, this road is to be built to be leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if it is a fact, as the Finance Minister assured the House, that the Grand Trunk Pacific cannot earn the interest upon that cost of construction the company will have to go bankrupt, although I presume the Grand Trunk Pacific Company know their business as well as the Minister of Finance knows it, or the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). The Grand Trunk Pacific must know their business as well as these gentlemen know it for them, and if they saw, from the cost of construction, that they were not going to be able to operate their railway and pay interest, surely they would have had something to say about the matter before now. But as a matter of fact the Grand Trunk Pacific Company are absolutely parties to that standard of construction, because the company wanted that standard and know that they have to pay the
interest on the cost. They are aware what the cost is from time to time, because their engineer has to pass upon the cost of every foot of the line. Now these hon. gentlemen have entertained the House at great length upon this question. I do not want to characterize their style of argument, because I am sure, Mr. Chairman, you would call me to order if I did. But when they say that the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific have so little knowledge of their business and so little regard for it that they would assist in carrying on that construction according to that standard with the results that they have suggested to this House, if they could impress the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company or the Grand Trunk Company with that idea there would surely be a change of management very quickly. The reputation of the management of both companies is that of men who thoroughly understand the railway business, and are able to make dividends out of railway traffic.
And I think that, so long as that matter is in the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the extent that it is, with the responsibilities resting upon the Grand Trunk Pacific as they do, these hon. gentlemen may make their minds easy and not worry about the ultimate result to the western producer or the eastern consumer, or producer either.
The prairie section of the Grand Trunk Pacific, it is said cost $40,000 a mile. Did the government pay that $40,000 a mile? The government guaranteed the bonds on $13,000 a mile, and the railway has to find the balance of $27,000 a mile in OTder to have a railway of the standard of this road across the prairies. Why .do they make a road of that high standard when they could have a road across the prairie for $13,000 to $15,000 a mile? Because they believed it would pay them to do it and just so they believe it will pay them to have the road from' Winnipeg east to Quebec and Moncton of such a standard as it is. For that standard is absolutely with the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has joined forces with the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) as the champion of the interests of the northwest. And he has added his word of advice to those of a good many other members of this House as to what the man in the northwest ought to do. Some people advise the man in the northwest to go into mixed farming; some people advise him to build granaries; some people advise him to raise chickens. But the Minister of Finance advises him to be an optimist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said he is an optimist.

If the hon. gentleman thinks that the man of the west lives on optimism, he is very much mistaken. If he thinks the western farmer is such an optimist that he likes to pay high railway rates, likes to have his grain tied up so that he cannot get it out, likes to be m such a position that he cannot pay his bills, likes to be compelled to pay an extra price for everything he buys-then my hon. friend is mistaken; the western farmer is not that kind of an optimist.
Why did you not remedy the difficulty during the fifteen years you were in power?

The Liberal government went out of power on a policy that meant remedying that condition; that is the very thing that put it out of power. And the late government has no apology to oner and no regrets to express that it went out of power on that issue. But never mind about the late government; it is to the present government that the people look for that relief which, according to their policy, this government denies it. My hon. friend told us that the late government was responsible for the grain blockades m the west because this Grand Trunk Pacific was not completed to Cochrane.
Because you did not build the Hudson Bay railway.

Did not do anything. Mr. OLIVER. If the road was completed to Cochrane, does not the hon. gentleman know that the grades on the Ontario railway from Cochrane to North Bay are such that the Grand Trunk Pacific to Cochrane would be only half the value that it would be otherwise ?
That is only what was built by the Ross government.
No, what was built by my hon. friend's (Mr. Cochrane) government.
No, the Ross government; that is the only grade there is.

At any rate the facts are as I have stated, that that road has to be completed to the city of Quebec according to the grades laid down before the whole line will be of the fullest benefit to the people of the west. It is true the road is not yet completed. It is also true that lion, members opposite, led by the present Prime Minister, held that arrangement up in parliament for one solid summer, held it back for a whole year; and that if that obstruction had not taken place in 1903, and if the same rate of construction had gone on that rules to-day, the road would have been linked up between Superior Junction and Cochrane. This connection would have been made and would have Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
proven valuable to the people of the west had it not been for the obstruction on that occasion.	,
There is no question that the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific will be of stupendous benefit to the west. There is no question that the Canadian Pacific railway which offers to-day the only connection, is a road of such grades and curves that no amount of money will ever make it so that it can haul grain to relieve the conditions that exist there to-day. The Canadian Pacific railway is not able to move two hundred cars a day over its line from Fort William eastward; and because of its inability to do this, it is not able even measurably to relieve the grain congestion that exists at thi's time.
' I was struck with the argument of the hon. Minister of Finance. At one period of his discourse he was explaining to us the fact that this Transcontinental railway running through the undeveloped country would have no local traffic, and in the next breath he complained because of the lack of optimism in regard to railway construction. Now, let me say to my hon. friend, who lives in Ontario, and represents Ontario more especially, that the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific through this very region that he talks about is the only thing that will add serious value to the greater part of that province of Ontario. If northern Ontario has any future at all that future will be absolutely created by the construction through it of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Furthermore, my hon. friend told us of the outlets that we should have, to the west, by Hudson bay, and to the east. A magnificent prospect, he said; a magnificent prospect truly; and every part or element of it a part of the policy of the late government, the very policy that he and his friends have been criticising and speaking of as a crime against Canada on this occasion and on previous occasions in this House.
The Ontario government subsidized the Canadian Northern before you did.

I am not speaking of the Canadian Northern railway, but of the Transcontinental. The Canadian Northern railway is another issue altogether. I say that the Grand Trunk Pacific is opening up what is called the clay belt of northern Ontario and giving value to that part of the country, at the expense of the Dominion government, and as a part of the policy of the late Liberal government.
You could not get there without going through Ontario, coulc you?

I presume it is just as desirable to open up Ontario as it is t<

open up any other part of the country, and if Ontario has 16,000,000 acres of valuable clay land in the northern part of the province, it is just as much a national enterprise to open that up to settlement as it is to open up any other part of the country.
Ontario can open that up herself.

Ontario did not, and under the present government, never would. There is no doubt that, the people of that northern part of Ontario to-day are so ill satisfied with the measure of development they received at the hands of the Minister of Railways and his colleagues, that they are to-day asking to be erected into a separate province in order to get their share of the Dominion subsidies to enable them to carry on their local business.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that in the last local election recently held, the present government carried thirteen seats out of 14 in new Ontario?
Yes, I am; I am not aware, however, of the methods by which they carried them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A word or two with regard to some matters the hon. gentleman has mentioned. He told us that the late government had no apology to offer for their defeat at the last election. Well, I am sure the country has no apology to offer for defeating them. He has stated that this contract was held up by a policy of obstruction in 1903. Is he aware at what date that contract was introduced?
I could not recollect the date at the moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He had better examine the dates before he makes a statement of that kind.
What was the date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The date was the 30th of July, and the session opened on the 12th of March.
When did it close?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It closed on the 24th of October, within two and a half months after the- greatest measure of the session was introduced, within two and a half months after effective discussion began on it. My hon. friend refers to that as obstruction. I say there was no obstruction, and the hon. gentleman has no warrant to say otherwise. The hon. gentleman has misquoted gentlemen on this side of the House very often in the course of his remarks. He said that hon. gentlemen on this side referred to the building o'f this road as a crime. They did not refer to it as a crime, they did refer to the inexcusable delay and the
methods of construction as a crime, and I entirely[DOT] agree with them in that estimate.
Would the Prime Minister then specify the criminal in the case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say it is absolutely inexcusable that they did not begin the construction of that road eastward from Superior Junction. Why was it any more difficult to do that than to undertake the construction of the road westward from Quebec ? Can any hon. gentleman explain that ? Why was it any more difficult to begin the construction of the road from Winnipeg eastward, than to begin the construction from Levis towards Moncton, or from Moncton towards Halifax? There is no distinction. Yet the hon. gentleman stands here, when he sees the result of that, and upholds the course of the late government, which undoubtedly now is having very serious consequences.
There must be some misunderstanding. I am under the impression that the construction was commenced eastward from Winnipeg.
It was the Lake Superior division.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I iaan referring to the particular portion of the road where there is now no prospect of completion within about two years, from Lake Superior to Cochrane.
The right hon. gentleman must be. in error. I know they commenced the construction from Winnipeg towards Superior Junction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am referring to the whole line from Winnipeg to Cochrane, There cannot be that outlet from Port Arthur to the east, which is absolutely necessary under present conditions.
But that is from Superior Junction eastwards, not from Winnipeg eastward.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I see no reason why thal road from Superior Junction to Cochrane could not have been proceeded with in just the same way as the road between Moncton and Levis.
The hon. gentleman said frem Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I did inadvertently use thal expression. I was referring to that particular portion of the line that will not b( completed for a year or two.
I asked the Prime Minis ter, if there was a criminal, Who was tin criminal ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why, my hon. friend and his colleagues.
Then it was not the commissioners' ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I will come to that at once. I stated here before that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals did not come here either to censure or to commend these commissioners, ancl the leader of the opposition nodded his approval, when I made that statement. He took the responsibility of introducing this measure as one which he thought to be in the public interest, having regard to the condition of the road, and having regard to the capacity of the man whom he placed there as chairman of the commission. This controversy about the work of the commissioners (has entirely arisen, as pointed out before, 'because hon. members on the other side of the House raised the question as to a certain allowance which should be made to these commissioners upon their retiring, and in the course of urging that this should be done, undertook to express very great commendation of the work which these gentlemen have performed. We had not criticised or said anything about them up to that time, but naturally, when that commendation was expressed, in possibly somewhat extravagant language, hon. gentlemen on this side of the House took exception to it, and in that way, the criticism has arisen, and it was solely due to the course taken by hon. gentlemen opposite. I have not come here, nor has the Minister of Railways come here, to commend or censure these commissioners; but we take the responsibility of saying that, having regard to the state of construction of this road, we think it eminently in the public interest that it should be completed under the man who has been appointed as chairman of that commission, and we take full responsibility. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was net, it seems to me, quite as fair as he usually is, when he made the statement with regard to the assistant to the chairman. He undertook to say that we proposed to pay the salary of two commissioners instead of four.
When any hon. gentleman undertakes to refer to place-hunters in respect to this commission, I want him to understand that the chairman of that commission very reluctantly undertook that work at my urgent and earnest request, and at the earnest request of the Minister of Railways. He did not seek it at 'all, he was not desirous of it, and the salary is a matter of absolute indifference to him. Every one who knows that gentleman knows that no such expression as that should have been used in regard to him.
I hope my hon. friend does not think I used it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Some hon. gentleman used it.
You used it.
No.
Not with reference to the chairman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know if it was with regard to him, but it was used. As a matter of fact, if we had followed the example of hon. gentlemen opposite we would have filled up the number of the commission even although we thought that it should not, be done. We reduced the number of commissioners from four to one, and appointed a man to whom the salary is a matter of utter indifference and who took the position simply with a desire to [perform a public service against his own interest and inclination. As to Mr. Mac-pherson, he was being paid before $5,000, and is being paid now $7,500, an increase of $2,500. In addition to the duties he was discharging before he is now discharging certain other responsible duties. From what I have heard of him, I believe he will give good value to the people for every dollar of salary which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) proposes to pay him.
The hon. member for Piotou made some rather remarkable statements 'about the report placed on the table by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) and used language with regard to it which means one of two tilings, either that the man who prepared it is incapable, or that he is dishonest. The man who prepared that statement is a man appointed by the late government byorder in council and the observations of my hon. friend in that regard are deserving of consideration.
To what does the hon. member refer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot quote his language but my hon. friend will see it in ' Hansard.' He criticised the statement in such terms as would indicate that the man who would make a statement of that kind to be submitted to parliament is not a man to be kept in the position ibe occupies.
I never said anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see his language in ' Hansard.'

I said the House was entitled to information as to how the three items were made up. I made no remarks of any kind on the subject beyond requesting that information. One hon. gentleman said he was our appointee. I said that that had nothing to do with the information I wanted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am bound to accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but that

is not how the matter impressed me, and if his statements are justified they are surely deserving of the attention of this government, and that necessary attention will be given to them.
What about the information and the details as to the three items, headquarters' salaries and expenses, engineering expenses, and right-of-way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We asked the man appointed to this responsible position by the late government for accurate and definite information in respect to these matters. If these items are not correct then that man appointed by the late government is responsible for their inaccuracy.
That answer was never good enough for the hon. gentleman when the tables were turned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In what case?
In any case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend will give a case I will be very glad to deal with it. All I have to say is that we have been relying on the statement of the responsible officer of these commissioners who was appointed by the late government. We are entitled to rely on that until it has been demonstrated to us that he is inaccurate, and we have presented the statement to the committee exactly in the manner in which he has presented it to us. My hon. friend repeated several times in the course of his speech that this road had been completed to the extent of 76 per cent. There is absolutely no warrant in this statement for any such assertion.
What is the mean; ing of the statement at the top of the page?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Exactly what it says, that the grading has been completed to that extent, but the hon. member knows that _ other matters are involved besides grading. When he says that the road has been completed to the extent of 76-86 per cent, he says what has absolutely no warrant in the statement produced, and he used that statement to make an argument which was absolutely unfair and improper from the statement as a whole. As a matter of fact, the road lias not been completed to the extent of 76 per cent. The giading has been completed to the extent of 76 per _ cent, the track has not been laid in anything like that proportion and any one who examined the items in this report will see that in several unimportant respects three-quarters ox nine-tenths of the work still remains to be done. Take the terminals at Quebec, $*>^8 500 have already been expended, there remains to be expended more than $9,000,000. Take car shops with their equipment, 109
'7! .000 have been expended, and there are $1,120,800 still to be expended. When any hon. gentleman finds fault with the report of this engineer, who is the engineer appointed by their own leader by order in council, and criticise his statement that the betterments during nine years from January 1, 1912 to December 3i;
I asked the Minister of Railways positively if Mr. Grant made that statement, and he would not say he did it. and I am satisfied it was Mr. Leonard who did it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend criticised it and wanted it struck out altogether.
I did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would give to my hon. friend some " information. The Grand Trunk Pacific has been completed and in running order from Winnipeg to Edmonton for I think about two years and has been carrying grain; and it is estimated *and I speak of what I know, that within the next two 5'ears the cost of betterments upon that road in order to complete it up to standai'd, will be just about the amount mentioned here as being required to be expended on this road within the next nine years.
It was not completed when it was taken over.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It has been in operation for two years carrying grain.
They commenced operating it before they had it completed.
Would the minister give an idea of the nature of the betterments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will apply to the Grand Trunk Pacific and they will take him into their confidence they can give him full particulars as to what the -proposed betterments aTe because in my statement I am relying on their representations -and that is precisely the statement that was made to us with regard to betterments that ought t-j be made upon this road during the next two or two and a half years. That road from Winnipeg to Edmonton is, I suppose, not much more than half the length of the line from Moncton to Winnipeg and the betterments proposed on that road in the next two or two and a half years are about equivalent to the sum which has been estimated by some one, Mr. Leonard or Mr. Grant, as being necessary to effect upon this road during the period of nine years after its completion.
Any hon. gentleman in this House who is familiar with the ordinary subsidence ox embankments, knows that no matter how perfectly you may build an embankment in the first instances, it will require



repair and betterment in order to bring it up to a standard when it will subside no more. You cannot build a road in the first instance so that it will absolutely require no betterment for a number of years.
Perhaps there is a distinction between betterments and repairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I aim not familiar with the technical distinction but I do say that no matter how well you may build a railroad in the first instance, it is absolutely necessary for solme years afterwards to spend money upon it for the purposes I have mentioned. That statement will commend itself to the common sense and judgment of every hon. member present.
I would like to allude to one other matter; a great deal has been said about tha original contract with the Canadian Pacific railway, and the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has informed us that the country gave away $800,000,000 according to his estimate, in land value. But, a great many hon. gentlemen who speak of that contract forget that their own leaders between 1874 and 1878 proposed a contract by which not 25,000,000 of acres but 50,000,000 of acres would be given away to any company that would construct the Canadian Pacific railway. If we apply the principle of valuation which my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) adopted, then the government of Mr. Alexander Mackenzie of which the present leader of the opposition was a member, was prepared to give away lands in western Canada worth $1,500,000,000. I would not be prepared to make any such absurd argument as that.
Neither would I.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend estimated these lands as being worth $30 per acre.
I said that the ten million acres remaining to be sold were worth $30 an acre and I say so now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend made an estimate of $800,000,000.
I did not say so. I said that the ten million acres still remaining were worth three hundred million dollars and ' Hansard5 will bear me out in that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I accept the statement of the hon. gentleman; I understood him to value these lands at $30 per acre.
Yes, the 10,000,000 acres remaining to be sold.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And 1 am simply remarking that if you applied the $30 per acre valuation 'to the 50,000,000 acres of land that were offered by the Mackenzie government-
But I did not apply it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: The hon. gentleman denied a statement the other night and ' Hansard ' showed he was wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better put it this way so as not to wound the feelings of my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell). If you apply a valuation of $30 an acre to the
50.000.	000 acres that were offered by the Mackenzie government you would have a sum of $1,500,000,000. I trust the statement in that form will not offend my hon. friend.
I don't object to that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to point out that section 8, subsection 3, of the Act which the Mackenzie government passed through this parliament, provided that a subsidy of $10,000 a mile for the 2,544 miles from North Bay to Vancouver, making altogether $25,440,000. In addition to that the Mackenzie government also offered a guarantee of interest at the rate of four per cent, for twenty-five years from tne completion of the work, on a sum to be agreed upon. As a matter of fact, the arrangement that was made by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald for the building of the Canadian Pacific railway was an infinitely better arrangement in the interest of the people of this country than the arrangement proposed by the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. Of course to-day, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House can talk glibly about lands that are worth $30 an acre, but those who know what the actual conditions were at the time the Canadian Pacific railway was commented in 1882 know that the Canadian Pacific railway would have been glad to hand these lands over at that time for fifty cents an acre; it would have been glad to get twelve and a half (million dollars instead of the>
25.000. 000 acres of land. Every ond in this country realizes1 that the conditions were then absolutely different from what they are to-day. It "is true that the lands did become very valuable afterwards, but in considering the fairness and reasonableness of the contract, we must estimate the conditions which confronted the country and the Canadian Pacific railway in 1882 and not the conditions as they are at the present time.
Well, we have wandered a good deal from the line of argument applicable to this Bill and perhaps some of my own observations are not pertinent to the actual question before the House, but I can only say that it is the belief of the government that the course which they are adopting in respect of this commission is in the public interest, and that the road can be effectively completed under the chairmanship and superintendence of Mr. Leonard. No effort will be spared^ to hurry that road on to completion.

and especially that part of it which is necessary in order that there may he a lime from Winnipeg to the east to afford an. opportunity to the people of the western country to get their grain out more effectively in the future than they have been able to do in the winter months in the past.

I would like this information .from the Minister of Railways. I do not want to be offensive, but I do hope he will not tell me again that the figures are Mr. Grant's. I know they are Mr. Grant's figures, but the hon. gentleman is here as the responsible head of the department, and we, as members of this House, have a right to ask for further information before the third reading of the Bill. For instance, in the statement submitted to the House, we are told that the rails .and fastenings, including frogs, switches and diamond crossings already completed amounted to $10,214,000, and that there remains to be done of this, work to the extent of $2,995,000, or in other words there is about thirty per cent of that work uncompleted. If you take the total mileage completed of 1,587 as against the total mileage of 1,803, you have only twenty-two per cent of that work to be done and perhaps the .minister will tell u.s wherein tire discrepancy comes. There is only twenity-two per cent of the track to be laid and it will cost thirty per cent of the total cost to do that.
I do not admit your statement. There .are the terminals and the sidings. We gave you the actual mileage where there is no track laid.

I am not including the 287 miles of sidings. There is also another point on which my hon. friend will probably bring ms further information, and that is in regard to the item of * engineering and expenses.' I find that under that 'head they have .spent already $7,681,000, and that the estimate is given that it will cost $3,850,000, or just exactly half as much is to be expended as has been expended.
We won't spend one dollar more than is necessary.

My hon. . friend will surely allow me to ask him a question. He states that they assume that they will be able to hand the road over by the 31st of December, 1913, in other words, in two years. The engineering end of this road has been in operation since 1905, that is, between six and seven years. Now, will the hon. gentleman tell us how his department figures that in two years we are going to require just half as much as we did in the last six years. The same thing applies to the headquarters expenditure, which in the last six years has amounted 109i
to $1,732,000, and they expect to spend in two years $1,260,000.
The hon. gentleman had better put in the right of way.

The light of way has not been settled in the same proportion in which the road has been built; yet I am satisfied that a good deal more than half of it has been settled. I am not finding any fault in regard to that. I think the Minister of Railways should not assume the attitude he does, because we have surely a right to ask for information. I admit that he is not in a position to give it to-night, but probably he will be able to do so when the Bill comes up for the third reading.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would remind my hon. friend that the information he asks for can be easily obtained and will be readily given [DOT]upon the estimates. It is not concerned with the passage of this Bill. We were asked to bring down a statement to corroborate the assertion of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, that the road was two-thirds or thereabouts completed. He has asked the engineer in charge of the work to make that statement, and it has been given, not only in general form, but in detail. So far as the expenditure of the money is concerned, that is a matter that can be dealt with on the estimates. when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways will be prepared to give the fullest information. We are entitled to rely on the statement of the engineer, appointed not by this government, but by the late government. Therefore I trust that my hon. friend from Carleton will be-content to have the information when the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals are before the House.

That may be all very well from the viewpoint of the Prime Minister, but it is not satisfactory to the opposition. The Minister of Railways persists in sitting in his seat like a bump on a log, absolutely refusing any information.
Order !

I did not intend to say that offensively, and if anybody on the other side thinks I did, I shall gladly withdraw it. But at least I wish to intimate to the Minister of Railways that he is not very courteous -or free in giving information that is asked of him by the opposition. He is following the example of the autocratic gentleman who lives in Queen's Park, Toronto, and if he does not look out he will be the exact type of that gentleman.
Thank you for that compliment.

The Prime Minister says that the information contained in this statement is irrelevant to the Bill before the House. That is true, but I want to call his attention to the fact that pretty nearly every hon. gentleman on the other side who has spoken on this Bill has urged, as the ground for the dismissal of scone of the commissioners, that the road has cost too much. In fact, after the statement of the minister the other night, the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) took the floor, and, with great indignation and in tones of contempt, declared most vehemently against the commissioners, who he thought were very lucky to secure a mere dismissal and in not having some proceedings, civil or criminal, taken against them. Now, in addition to what is asked for by the hon. member for Car-leton, I would like the Minister of Railways when the Bill is next before the House, to state whether it was intended by this statement to lead the House to believe that the first seven years of interest after the construction of the eastern section which is being handed over to the Transcontinental Railway Commission, was to constitute a part , of the capital on which the government was to charge interest against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
The contract says that it does not.

1 think it is quite clear that it is not part of the capital on which the interest is to be calculated; but I understood, from some hon. gentlemen who spoke this evening, that [DOT]that seven years' interest was to be added to the capital. If the Minister of Railways is satisfied that it is not, I am content with that.

I called the attention of the Prime Minister to the question of the legality of the appointment of Mr. Macpherson. I am very much impressed with the view that his appointment could not legally be made in the way it was. and I had hoped that when he spoke he would have dealt with that. Unless he is in a position to discuss that now, I would like to hear about it on the third reading of the Bill.

With reference to the appointment of Mr. Macpherson, the law clerk of the Commission advised Mr. Leonard that he had the power to make the appointment. Mr. Mclsaac, one of the commissioners, advised the same tiling, and the Commission as a whole, in . Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
passing the estimates for the payment of Mr Macpherson, in that way confirmed it.

I do not think that was good enough.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Order No. 28, Public Bills and Orders, is a resolution standing in the name of the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). Since the resolution was last discussed there has been no opportunity of calling it except on one occasion when the Postmaster General had to be absent. The hon. gentleman is desirous of not being hampered by having the resolution on the order paper where it cannot be discussed without the consent of the House. I, therefore, move that order No. 28 be called for the purpose of having the resolution withdrawn. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) desires to discuss some of the matters that are embraced within this resolution. A day or two ago when he proposed to do that, the point of order was raised, and it was considered that with the unanimous consent of the House he might go on. However, I think it will be better to proceed in. the regular way. It is for that reason I move the resolution.
Under what circumstances will the discussion come on?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The discussion will come on at any time the member for Rouville is desirous of raising it, when we go into Supply as I understand.
I do not understand that the member for Rouville would have the bringing up of the subject. I was debating the subject and was going to bring it up myself.

Motion agreed to.
Mr ARMSTRONG moved, seconded by Mr. Lennox, that order No. 28 be discharged.
Motion agreed to.

There is a resolution under the heading of government notices of motion in regard to the Manitoba Boundaries. Would it be possible to lay on the table the correspondence in connection with this matter, beginning with the conference that was held between the Premiers of Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and the Prime Minister of Canada, and covering the period from that time forward to the present?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have already given instructions that the order of the House

which has already been made in that regard, be complied with before the resolution is brought on.
Mr. BORDEN moved the adjournment of the Blouse.
What is the order of business for to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We expect to take up government Bills, beginning with the Grain Bill, and after that Supply, proceeding with the estimates of the Minister of the Interior.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.50 a.m., Tuesday.
Tuesday, February 20, 1912.
